metadata.title: The course says that by the end you will know four purification met...

variants.stem: The course says that by the end you will know four purification methods and when to use each. Which set is it?
variants.explanation:
**Distillation, recrystallisation, chromatography and sublimation.** These are the four named on p.3. In the six lab experiments you use recrystallisation most often, column chromatography in Expt 7 and sublimation in Expt 5E; distillation (including under reduced pressure) is taught through the technique videos.

Why the others fail:
- **Distillation, recrystallisation, extraction and filtration**: Extraction and filtration are separation operations used in work-ups, not the four purification methods the manual lists.
- **Recrystallisation, chromatography, titration and sublimation**: Titration measures an amount; it does not purify a product.
- **Distillation, chromatography, melting-point determination and sublimation**: A melting point characterises a solid (it shows purity) but does not purify it.

*Source: Manual p.3.*

options.label: Distillation, recrystallisation, chromatography and sublimation
Distillation, recrystallisation, extraction and filtration
Recrystallisation, chromatography, titration and sublimation
Distillation, chromatography, melting-point determination and sublimation

metadata.title: A crude product is a mixture of three coloured organometallic compo...
metadata.source: Manual p.3 (the four methods); matching them to the experiments: pp.29-47

variants.stem: A crude product is a mixture of three coloured organometallic compounds of different polarity, a few hundred milligrams in all. Which purification method fits?
variants.explanation:
**Column chromatography.** It separates components by how strongly they stick to silica; the polarity differences are exactly what Expt 7 exploits.

Why the others fail:
- **Recrystallisation from one solvent**: It removes small amounts of impurity from one major solid; three comparable components would co-crystallise or be lost in the mother liquor.
- **Simple distillation**: These are solids, not liquids with well-separated boiling points.
- **Washing with water**: The compounds are organic and not water-soluble, so water separates none of them.

*Source: Manual p.3 (the four methods); matching them to the experiments: pp.29-47.*

options.label: Column chromatography
Recrystallisation from one solvent
Simple distillation
Washing with water

variants.stem: A small amount of a volatile, low-melting solid must be freed from non-volatile solid by-products. Which method does the manual use for this in Expt 5E?
variants.explanation:
**Sublimation under vacuum with gentle warming.** The product passes straight from solid to vapour onto the cold finger and leaves the non-volatile material behind.

Why the others fail:
- **Column chromatography on silica**: Possible in principle but not the method the manual uses, and wasteful for a clean volatile solid.
- **Recrystallisation from hot water**: The manual does not use it for this product; sublimation avoids solvent and losses in the mother liquor.
- **Distillation at atmospheric pressure**: The product is a solid, and the manual sublimes it under about 6 mmHg with heating of at most 50 °C, far gentler than atmospheric distillation.

*Source: Manual p.3 (the four methods); matching them to the experiments: pp.29-47.*

options.label: Sublimation under vacuum with gentle warming
Column chromatography on silica
Recrystallisation from hot water
Distillation at atmospheric pressure

variants.stem: A product is a solid that dissolves well in hot ethanol and poorly in cold ethanol, with small amounts of coloured impurity. Which method is the usual choice?
variants.explanation:
**Recrystallisation.** The large solubility change with temperature is what recrystallisation needs; impurities stay in the cold solvent.

Why the others fail:
- **Sublimation**: It needs a solid that is volatile; solubility behaviour is irrelevant to it.
- **Distillation**: Distillation is for liquids; this product is a solid purified by dissolving and recrystallising.
- **Column chromatography**: It works, but is slower and uses much more solvent than the simple method that fits this solubility pattern.

*Source: Manual p.3 (the four methods); matching them to the experiments: pp.29-47.*

options.label: Recrystallisation
Sublimation
Distillation
Column chromatography

metadata.title: In the course workflow "synthesise, purify, characterise", what is ...

variants.stem: In the course workflow "synthesise, purify, characterise", what is the aim of the characterise stage?
variants.explanation:
**To show that the material is both the right compound and pure.** The manual says you must demonstrate that what you made is the desired product and is pure, using mp, TLC, IR and NMR.

Why the others fail:
- **To increase the yield of the crude product**: Yield is set in the synthesis; characterisation measures, it does not make more product.
- **To remove the last traces of solvent**: Drying is part of purification; characterisation only analyses the result.
- **To check that the procedure was followed in the notebook**: Following the procedure belongs to the first stage; this stage is about the product itself.

*Source: Manual p.4.*

options.label: To show that the material is both the right compound and pure
To increase the yield of the crude product
To remove the last traces of solvent
To check that the procedure was followed in the notebook

metadata.title: Who does what with the NMR and IR spectra in CM2061?

variants.stem: Who does what with the NMR and IR spectra in CM2061?
variants.explanation:
**You run the IR yourself; the NMR is recorded for you after a TA helps with the sample, and you process, print and interpret it.** The manual makes processing (Fourier transform, printing, expansions) and interpretation your responsibility; Spinworks is one option, any software is allowed.

Why the others fail:
- **The TA runs and interprets both spectra for you**: You record the IR yourself and you interpret both; only the NMR acquisition is done for you.
- **You run both spectrometers unaided**: Students submit NMR samples with a TA's help and do not run the spectrometer (even licence holders submit samples).
- **You run the NMR yourself and the TA records the IR**: The roles are the other way round: IR is yours, NMR acquisition is the staff's.

*Source: Manual pp.4, 15-16.*

options.label: You run the IR yourself; the NMR is recorded for you after a TA helps with the sample, and you process, print and interpret it
The TA runs and interprets both spectra for you
You run both spectrometers unaided
You run the NMR yourself and the TA records the IR

metadata.title: Benzene is both a carcinogen and flammable. How should this appear ...

variants.stem: Benzene is both a carcinogen and flammable. How should this appear in the pre-lab risk assessment?
variants.explanation:
**As two separate hazards, each with its own precaution.** A hazard is a property of a chemical, not the chemical itself, and different properties need different precautions.

Why the others fail:
- **As one entry, "benzene: dangerous", with a single precaution**: This names the chemical, not a property, and one precaution cannot cover both properties.
- **Only the more serious property is listed**: The table asks for three hazards of the experiment, so a second property of the same chemical can fill another row; it should not be dropped just because it is less serious.
- **Benzene need not be listed because it is a solvent**: Being a solvent does not remove its hazards; the table is for the most serious risks of the experiment.

*Source: Manual p.7.*

options.label: As two separate hazards, each with its own precaution
As one entry, "benzene: dangerous", with a single precaution
Only the more serious property is listed
Benzene need not be listed because it is a solvent

metadata.title: Which row is written correctly for a risk assessment (hazard, then ...

variants.stem: Which row is written correctly for a risk assessment (hazard, then precaution)?
variants.explanation:
**Diethyl ether is flammable; use it in the fume cupboard with no naked flames or sources of ignition.** It names a property (flammable) and gives a precaution that addresses that property.

Why the others fail:
- **Diethyl ether; wear goggles**: No hazard is named, and goggles are required for every experiment, so this is not a precaution specific to the hazard.
- **Sulfuric acid is a chemical; be careful**: A chemical is not a hazard, and "be careful" is not a precaution.
- **Flammable, corrosive and toxic; use the fume cupboard**: Separate hazards need separate precautions; one precaution cannot address all three properties.

*Source: Manual p.7.*

options.label: Diethyl ether is flammable; use it in the fume cupboard with no naked flames or sources of ignition
Diethyl ether; wear goggles
Sulfuric acid is a chemical; be careful
Flammable, corrosive and toxic; use the fume cupboard

metadata.title: How many hazards must the pre-lab risk assessment identify for an e...

variants.stem: How many hazards must the pre-lab risk assessment identify for an experiment, and what goes with each?
variants.explanation:
**Three hazards, each with one reasonable precaution.** The manual's table has three rows, and the learning outcomes say you consider "three risks, not one".

Why the others fail:
- **One hazard, the most dangerous, with every precaution you can think of**: The task is breadth: three different hazards, one precaution each.
- **Every hazard of every chemical, with a full safety data sheet**: The table is a short list of the most serious risks, not an exhaustive inventory.
- **Three hazards with three precautions each**: One reasonable precaution per hazard is what the table asks for.

*Source: Manual pp.3, 7.*

options.label: Three hazards, each with one reasonable precaution
One hazard, the most dangerous, with every precaution you can think of
Every hazard of every chemical, with a full safety data sheet
Three hazards with three precautions each

metadata.title: A TA looks at your completed risk assessment before you start. What...

variants.stem: A TA looks at your completed risk assessment before you start. What does that inspection establish?
variants.explanation:
**Only that the assessment has been done, not that it is correct.** The manual says the inspection ensures it was done; being correct is still your responsibility.

Why the others fail:
- **That every hazard and precaution is correct**: The manual explicitly says the inspection does not check correctness.
- **That you may skip the safety quiz**: The safety video and test are separate requirements for working in the lab at all.
- **That the experiment is approved for repetition if it goes wrong**: Repeats need permission from the course coordinator and lab staff, and have nothing to do with the risk assessment.

*Source: Manual p.7.*

options.label: Only that the assessment has been done, not that it is correct
That every hazard and precaution is correct
That you may skip the safety quiz
That the experiment is approved for repetition if it goes wrong

metadata.title: You wear prescription glasses to the lab. What eye protection is re...

variants.stem: You wear prescription glasses to the lab. What eye protection is required?
variants.explanation:
**Safety goggles worn over the glasses.** Ordinary glasses do not give adequate protection, so goggles go over them, at all times.

Why the others fail:
- **Your glasses are enough because they cover the eyes**: The manual states that ordinary glasses do not provide adequate protection.
- **Goggles only when handling corrosive reagents**: Goggles must be worn at all times in the lab, not just for dangerous steps.
- **Swap to contact lenses and wear goggles over them**: Contact lenses must not be worn in the lab even under goggles.

*Source: Manual p.8.*

options.label: Safety goggles worn over the glasses
Your glasses are enough because they cover the eyes
Goggles only when handling corrosive reagents
Swap to contact lenses and wear goggles over them

metadata.title: Why are contact lenses forbidden even when safety goggles are worn?

variants.stem: Why are contact lenses forbidden even when safety goggles are worn?
variants.explanation:
**Corrosive material can flow under the edge of the lens, and a lens hinders immediate, complete flushing of the eye.** Both reasons are given on p.8: permanent damage can result.

Why the others fail:
- **Lenses are flammable and would catch fire from a hot plate**: Nothing in the manual says this; the concern is chemical splashes and flushing.
- **Goggles fog up more when lenses are worn**: Comfort is not the issue; eye injury is.
- **Lenses react with organic solvent vapour and release toxic gas**: The risk is a splash trapped under the lens, not a reaction of the lens itself.

*Source: Manual p.8.*

options.label: Corrosive material can flow under the edge of the lens, and a lens hinders immediate, complete flushing of the eye
Lenses are flammable and would catch fire from a hot plate
Goggles fog up more when lenses are worn
Lenses react with organic solvent vapour and release toxic gas

metadata.title: A fume cupboard in the teaching lab starts to sound a whining alarm...

variants.stem: A fume cupboard in the teaching lab starts to sound a whining alarm. What is the cause and the fix?
variants.explanation:
**The sash is up too far, so the cupboard is not protecting you; pull the sash down.** The alarm sounds when the sash is left too far up, and the same applies to a shared waste-solvent cupboard.

Why the others fail:
- **The extraction fan has failed; leave it running and carry on**: The manual ties the alarm to the sash position, and a cupboard in that state cannot protect you, so you must not carry on.
- **Solvent has been spilt inside; mop it up**: The alarm is a sash-height alarm, not a spill detector.
- **The fire alarm has been triggered; evacuate**: A fume-cupboard alarm is separate from the fire alarm.

*Source: Manual p.10.*

options.label: The sash is up too far, so the cupboard is not protecting you; pull the sash down
The extraction fan has failed; leave it running and carry on
Solvent has been spilt inside; mop it up
The fire alarm has been triggered; evacuate

metadata.title: Which student would be allowed into the teaching lab?

variants.stem: Which student would be allowed into the teaching lab?
variants.explanation:
**Lab coat, long trousers, closed shoes with no gap to the trousers, long hair tied back.** It meets every rule: coat, long pants, full-coverage shoes and tied-back hair.

Why the others fail:
- **Lab coat, Bermuda shorts, closed shoes**: Shorts of any kind (including Bermudas) are not permitted.
- **Lab coat, long trousers, sandals**: Sandals, slippers, open-toed and high-heeled shoes are not allowed.
- **Lab coat, long skirt, closed shoes**: Skirts may not be worn; long pants are required.

*Source: Manual pp.8, 10.*

options.label: Lab coat, long trousers, closed shoes with no gap to the trousers, long hair tied back
Lab coat, Bermuda shorts, closed shoes
Lab coat, long trousers, sandals
Lab coat, long skirt, closed shoes

metadata.title: Which use of a phone is permitted in the teaching lab?

variants.stem: Which use of a phone is permitted in the teaching lab?
variants.explanation:
**Watching an experiment video via its QR code.** This is the single exception: videos only (and gloves must come off before touching the phone).

Why the others fail:
- **Listening to music through earphones while you stir**: Personal audio equipment is banned because anything that interferes with hearing what is going on is a hazard.
- **Replying to messages between steps**: Electronic items are not permitted except for the lab videos.
- **Photographing your apparatus for the report**: Only video viewing is allowed; photos are not mentioned as an exception.

*Source: Manual pp.8-9.*

options.label: Watching an experiment video via its QR code
Listening to music through earphones while you stir
Replying to messages between steps
Photographing your apparatus for the report

metadata.title: The lab starts at 9:30 am. What happens if you arrive at 9:45?

variants.stem: The lab starts at 9:30 am. What happens if you arrive at 9:45?
variants.explanation:
**You may be refused entry and receive zero marks for that session.** More than 10 minutes late risks exclusion and a zero for the session.

Why the others fail:
- **You enter normally and lose a few marks for lateness only**: Lateness up to 10 minutes can cost behaviour marks; beyond 10 minutes you may be excluded with zero.
- **You may enter but must skip the risk assessment**: The risk assessment is never skipped, and the manual makes no such concession.
- **You are moved to the Friday group automatically**: Swapping groups needs permission from the coordinator or lab staff.

*Source: Manual p.11.*

options.label: You may be refused entry and receive zero marks for that session
You enter normally and lose a few marks for lateness only
You may enter but must skip the risk assessment
You are moved to the Friday group automatically

metadata.title: The procedure says to stir for two hours. Can you leave the bench f...

variants.stem: The procedure says to stir for two hours. Can you leave the bench for lunch during that time?
variants.explanation:
**Yes, if the reaction is safe and stable while unattended; ask a TA if unsure.** The manual encourages planning lunch around stirring or refluxing, provided it is safe.

Why the others fail:
- **No, the reaction must be watched every minute**: The manual says you can leave it while stirring or refluxing if safe.
- **Yes, but only after switching off the stirrer**: Stopping the stirrer defeats the two-hour step; the point is to leave it running safely.
- **Only if another student signs a form**: No such form is mentioned; the test is safety and a TA's advice.

*Source: Manual p.11.*

options.label: Yes, if the reaction is safe and stable while unattended; ask a TA if unsure
No, the reaction must be watched every minute
Yes, but only after switching off the stirrer
Only if another student signs a form

metadata.title: Which of these is listed as unethical behaviour?

variants.stem: Which of these is listed as unethical behaviour?
variants.explanation:
**Claiming a higher yield than you actually obtained.** Pretending you got a higher yield is on the manual's list, with copying reports and using others' data.

Why the others fail:
- **Discussing the chemistry with your neighbours at the bench**: The manual encourages discussing chemistry and learning from neighbours' activities.
- **Reading the procedures of experiments you were not assigned**: The manual advises this, since the exam can ask about all versions.
- **Asking a TA whether a piece of advice is sound**: You are meant to judge advice critically, and asking is fine.

*Source: Manual pp.5, 14.*

options.label: Claiming a higher yield than you actually obtained
Discussing the chemistry with your neighbours at the bench
Reading the procedures of experiments you were not assigned
Asking a TA whether a piece of advice is sound

metadata.title: Where does the thick cardboard sheet from the back of the lab noteb...

variants.stem: Where does the thick cardboard sheet from the back of the lab notebook go before you write?
variants.explanation:
**Between the carbon copy of the current page and the standard copy of the next page.** It stops the carbon copies of the following pages being etched by the pressure of your pen.

Why the others fail:
- **Between the standard copy and the carbon copy of the page you are writing on**: That would stop the carbon copy from forming at all; the sheet goes behind the carbon, protecting the pages that follow.
- **Under the back cover so the book lies flat**: It has a specific job inside the book, shielding the next pages from etching.
- **Torn out and handed in with the carbon copy**: It is a working shield, not something you submit; you tear out only the carbon copy.

*Source: Manual p.12.*

options.label: Between the carbon copy of the current page and the standard copy of the next page
Between the standard copy and the carbon copy of the page you are writing on
Under the back cover so the book lies flat
Torn out and handed in with the carbon copy

metadata.title: At the end of the lab day, what do you hand in from your notebook?

variants.stem: At the end of the lab day, what do you hand in from your notebook?
variants.explanation:
**Only the carbon copy of each page for that day's experiment, signed by a TA, before leaving the lab.** You tear out just the carbon copies, with a TA signature at the bottom, and submit them to the document box before leaving.

Why the others fail:
- **The standard (top) copies, since they are the clearer ones**: You keep the standard copies and submit the carbon copies.
- **Both copies of every page in the notebook**: Only the pages for that day's experiment, and only the carbon copy of each.
- **Nothing; the notebook page is attached to the lab report online**: The carbon copy must be dropped in the box before you leave, and a copy of the page is also attached to the report; neither replaces the other.

*Source: Manual p.12.*

options.label: Only the carbon copy of each page for that day's experiment, signed by a TA, before leaving the lab
The standard (top) copies, since they are the clearer ones
Both copies of every page in the notebook
Nothing; the notebook page is attached to the lab report online

metadata.title: Which lab report would be marked?

variants.stem: Which lab report would be marked?
variants.explanation:
**Answers typed into the current proforma, with IR, NMR and the notebook page combined into one PDF, structures in bond-line style.** This follows every rule on pp.12-13.

Why the others fail:
- **A neatly handwritten report, photographed and uploaded**: Handwritten, scanned or photographed reports are not marked and graded zero.
- **A retyped copy of last year's proforma with your answers**: Only the current proformas downloaded from the experiment LAMS sequence are accepted; re-typed versions score zero.
- **The proforma plus the spectra as three separate uploads**: Everything must be combined into a single PDF, or it is not accepted.

*Source: Manual pp.12-13.*

options.label: Answers typed into the current proforma, with IR, NMR and the notebook page combined into one PDF, structures in bond-line style
A neatly handwritten report, photographed and uploaded
A retyped copy of last year's proforma with your answers
The proforma plus the spectra as three separate uploads

metadata.title: How is the CM2061 grade divided?

variants.stem: How is the CM2061 grade divided?
variants.explanation:
**Final exam 50%, lab reports 30%, e-labs 15%, LAMS quizzes 5%.** These are the weights in the table on p.12; you must also complete all six in-lab experiments to sit the exam.

Why the others fail:
- **Final exam 70%, lab reports 30%**: The e-labs (15%) and LAMS quizzes (5%) carry marks and the exam is 50%.
- **Final exam 50%, lab reports 50%**: Reports are 30%; e-labs and quizzes make up the other 20%.
- **Final exam 30%, lab reports 50%, e-labs 20%**: The weights are reversed: the exam is the largest part, at 50%.

*Source: Manual p.12.*

options.label: Final exam 50%, lab reports 30%, e-labs 15%, LAMS quizzes 5%
Final exam 70%, lab reports 30%
Final exam 50%, lab reports 50%
Final exam 30%, lab reports 50%, e-labs 20%

metadata.title: A balance displays 16.1323 g for your crude product. How do you rep...

variants.stem: A balance displays 16.1323 g for your crude product. How do you report the mass?
variants.explanation:
**16.132 g.** Masses are given to 3 significant figures but never to less than a whole milligram, so the 3 s.f. value of 16.1 g is too coarse; the milligram is the finest digit justified.

Why the others fail:
- **16.1 g**: Three significant figures alone would give this, but the rule adds "not less than a whole mg": 16.1 g throws away more than a milligram.
- **16.1323 g**: The extra digits come from the instrument, not from real precision; the manual warns that digital read-outs give too many figures.
- **16.13 g**: This rounds to the nearest 10 mg, which is coarser than the whole-mg limit.

*Source: Manual p.14.*

variants.stem: The yield of a reaction calculates as 71.46%. How should it be reported?
variants.explanation:
**71%.** Yields are quoted as a whole percentage.

Why the others fail:
- **71.5%**: One decimal place is more precision than the rule allows.
- **71.46%**: The raw calculator value claims accuracy that the measurements do not have.
- **70%**: Rounding to the nearest ten is coarser than the whole-percent rule.

*Source: Manual p.14.*

variants.stem: A product melts over 169.4 to 171.2 °C. How is the melting-point range reported?
variants.explanation:
**169-171 °C.** Melting points are quoted to the nearest whole degree, so each end of the range is rounded to a whole degree.

Why the others fail:
- **169.4-171.2 °C**: Tenths of a degree are not justified on this apparatus; the rule is the nearest whole degree.
- **170 °C**: Quoting one number discards the range, and the range tells you about purity.
- **169.0-171.0 °C**: Adding ".0" implies the tenths place was measured, which it was not.

*Source: Manual p.14.*

variants.stem: Which value is reported to the accuracy the manual asks for?
variants.explanation:
**δ 7.26 and J = 8.1 Hz.** Chemical shifts are given to 2 decimal places and coupling constants to 1.

Why the others fail:
- **δ 7.3 and J = 8.1 Hz**: The shift needs two decimal places.
- **δ 7.26 and J = 8 Hz**: J needs one decimal place.
- **δ 7.264 and J = 8.12 Hz**: Both are too precise: 2 d.p. for δ and 1 d.p. for J.

*Source: Manual p.14.*

options.label: δ 7.26 and J = 8.1 Hz
δ 7.3 and J = 8.1 Hz
δ 7.26 and J = 8 Hz
δ 7.264 and J = 8.12 Hz

variants.stem: The instrument gives an IR band at 1687.4 cm⁻¹ and an Rf of 0.4321. Which pair is reported correctly?
variants.explanation:
**1687 cm⁻¹ and Rf 0.43.** IR frequencies go to the nearest whole wavenumber and Rf to 2 decimal places.

Why the others fail:
- **1687.4 cm⁻¹ and Rf 0.4**: Neither is right: the IR needs a whole number and Rf needs 2 d.p.
- **1690 cm⁻¹ and Rf 0.43**: The IR value is rounded to the nearest 10 rather than the nearest whole wavenumber.
- **1687 cm⁻¹ and Rf 0.432**: Rf is given to 2 decimal places, not 3.

*Source: Manual p.14.*

options.label: 1687 cm⁻¹ and Rf 0.43
1687.4 cm⁻¹ and Rf 0.4
1690 cm⁻¹ and Rf 0.43
1687 cm⁻¹ and Rf 0.432

variants.stem: A pressure gauge on the vacuum line reads 5.8 mmHg (to a tenth). How should the pressure be reported?
variants.explanation:
**6 mmHg.** Pressure is reported to a whole mmHg.

Why the others fail:
- **5.8 mmHg**: Tenths are not justified for this gauge; the rule says whole mmHg.
- **5 mmHg**: Truncating instead of rounding gives the wrong value; 5.8 rounds to 6.
- **0.0058 mmHg**: This changes the number itself, not just the way it is quoted.

*Source: Manual p.14.*

options.label: 6 mmHg
5.8 mmHg
5 mmHg
0.0058 mmHg

variants.stem: A solution has a measured optical rotation which you convert to a specific rotation of +41.2873. How is [α]D reported?
variants.explanation:
**+41.3.** [α]D is given to 1 decimal place.

Why the others fail:
- **+41**: One decimal place is required, so a whole number is too coarse.
- **+41.29**: Two decimal places is too many for this quantity.
- **+41.2873**: This is the unrounded calculator display.

*Source: Manual p.14.*

variants.stem: You calculate that a reaction used 0.0067842 mol of a reagent. How many moles do you quote?
variants.explanation:
**0.00678 mol (6.78 mmol).** Moles are quoted to 3 significant figures.

Why the others fail:
- **0.0068 mol**: That is only 2 significant figures.
- **0.006784 mol**: That is 4 significant figures, one too many.
- **0.01 mol**: This rounds far too coarsely and wastes the measurement.

*Source: Manual p.14.*

options.label: 0.01 mol

metadata.title: Which quantity is reported to two decimal places according to the a...

variants.stem: Which quantity is reported to two decimal places according to the accuracy table?
variants.explanation:
**Molecular mass (and magnetic moment, Rf and 1H NMR shift).** The table gives 2 d.p. for molecular mass, magnetic moment, Rf and δ; coupling constants and [α]D get 1.

Why the others fail:
- **Yield**: A whole percentage.
- **Boiling point**: Boiling points are given to the nearest whole degree.
- **Coupling constant J**: J has one decimal place.

*Source: Manual p.14.*

options.label: Molecular mass (and magnetic moment, Rf and 1H NMR shift)
Yield
Boiling point
Coupling constant J

metadata.title: Which type of article is a fast announcement of a new discovery wit...

variants.stem: Which type of article is a fast announcement of a new discovery with a limited amount of experimental detail?
variants.explanation:
**A communication.** It is short, quick and may have few examples; a full paper follows with details.

Why the others fail:
- **A review**: A review discusses existing literature and has no new results.
- **A full paper**: A full paper is the thorough investigation with a good number of examples and full experimental details.
- **A textbook chapter**: Textbooks are secondary literature that rely on published papers.

*Source: Manual pp.26-27.*

options.label: A communication
A review
A full paper
A textbook chapter

variants.stem: Which of these is primary literature?
variants.explanation:
**A full paper reporting new results.** Communications and full papers contain new results, so they are primary.

Why the others fail:
- **A review article**: Reviews rely on earlier papers, so they are secondary.
- **A textbook such as Comprehensive Organic Synthesis**: Textbooks are secondary literature.
- **The Dictionary of Organic Compounds**: It is a reference collection built from the literature, so it is secondary.

*Source: Manual pp.26-27.*

options.label: A full paper reporting new results
A review article
A textbook such as Comprehensive Organic Synthesis
The Dictionary of Organic Compounds

variants.stem: Which of these journals publishes reviews only?
variants.explanation:
**Chemical Reviews.** Chem. Rev. (ACS) and Chem. Soc. Rev. (RSC) are marked as reviews only.

Why the others fail:
- **Organic Letters**: Org. Lett. publishes communications.
- **Tetrahedron**: Tetrahedron takes both reviews and papers.
- **Synlett**: Synlett (Thieme) publishes communications.

*Source: Manual pp.26-27.*

options.label: Chemical Reviews
Organic Letters
Tetrahedron
Synlett

variants.stem: Which journal and publisher are correctly paired?
variants.explanation:
**Tetrahedron Letters, Elsevier.** Tetrahedron and Tetrahedron Lett. are Elsevier titles; the latter carries communications.

Why the others fail:
- **Synthesis, Wiley-VCH**: Synthesis and Synlett are published by Thieme.
- **Chemical Communications, the American Chemical Society**: Chem. Commun. is a Royal Society of Chemistry journal.
- **Inorganic Chemistry, Elsevier**: Inorg. Chem. is an ACS journal.

*Source: Manual pp.26-27.*

options.label: Tetrahedron Letters, Elsevier
Synthesis, Wiley-VCH

variants.explanation:
**Wiley-VCH.** The manual lists Angewandte Chemie, Chemistry (a European and an Asian Journal) and Advanced Synthesis and Catalysis under Wiley-VCH.

Why the others fail:
- **Elsevier**: Elsevier lists Tetrahedron and Tetrahedron Letters.
- **Thieme**: Thieme lists Synthesis and Synlett.
- **The American Chemical Society**: ACS lists JACS, JOC, Org. Lett., Chem. Rev. and Inorg. Chem.

variants.stem: Which element must NOT appear in an ACS-format citation of a chemistry journal paper as CM2061 uses it?
variants.explanation:
**The title of the paper.** Chemistry journals (almost always) omit the paper title; biologists usually include it.

Why the others fail:
- **The first page number**: The first page is required.
- **The year**: The year is required (in bold).
- **The volume**: The volume is required (in italics), where the journal has one.

*Source: Manual p.27.*

variants.stem: Which reference is acceptable in a CM2061 lab report?
variants.explanation:
**Hegedus, L. S.; Bates, R. W.; Soderberg, B. C. J. Am. Chem. Soc. 1991, 113, 923-927.** It cites a journal paper with authors (family name, initials), abbreviated journal, year, volume and pages.

Why the others fail:
- **https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/chemistry/1912/summary/**: Citations must be to journals, not web pages.
- **Hegedus; Bates; Soderberg. J. Am. Chem. Soc. 113 (3), 1991.**: It lacks initials and pages, and quotes an issue number the format does not need.
- **Wikipedia, "Grignard reagent", retrieved last week.**: A web page, not a journal paper; the manual says no www.

*Source: Manual p.27.*

variants.stem: In the citation format, how are the authors written?
variants.explanation:
**Family name then initials, authors separated by semicolons, no comma before the journal.** The example reads "Hegedus, L.S.; Bates, R.W.; Soderberg, B.C. J. Am. Chem. Soc."

Why the others fail:
- **Initials then family name, separated by commas**: The order is family name first, and semicolons separate authors.
- **First author only, then "et al."**: The manual's example lists all authors.
- **Full first names in alphabetical order**: The format uses initials, in the order they appear on the paper.

*Source: Manual p.27.*

metadata.title: You need all papers by a named author on a particular topic. Which ...

variants.stem: You need all papers by a named author on a particular topic. Which NTU resource is suited, and why?
variants.explanation:
**Scopus, which searches by author and keyword but cannot search by molecule.** The manual says Scopus finds particular authors and topics, not molecules.

Why the others fail:
- **Scopus, because it lets you draw a structure to search**: It cannot search for molecules; Reaxys and SciFinder can.
- **A general web search, because it is faster**: Search engines cover the whole internet and can return wrong chemistry (the lead styphnate example).
- **The Dictionary of Organic Compounds, which indexes every paper**: It lists only a few thousand compounds and is not a paper index.

*Source: Manual p.28.*

variants.stem: Which statement about Reaxys is correct?
variants.explanation:
**It is the online Beilstein (organic) and Gmelin (inorganic) database and allows structure drawing as a search.** The manual presents Reaxys as the German-origin counterpart to SciFinder, good for molecules and reactions.

Why the others fail:
- **It is the American Chemical Society's abstract service**: That description fits SciFinder (the CAS database), not Reaxys.
- **It cannot search for reactions**: It is "very useful for finding particular molecules and reactions".
- **It holds only a few thousand organic compounds**: That is the size of the Chapman and Hall dictionaries on chemnetbase, not Reaxys.

*Source: Manual p.28.*

variants.stem: In the chemnetbase dictionaries, how should a molecular formula be written to find a compound by formula?
variants.explanation:
**C first, then H, then all other elements alphabetically (p-toluenesulfonyl chloride: C7H7ClO2S).** This is the stated rule: C, then H, then everything else in alphabetical order.

Why the others fail:
- **In the usual chemical order, e.g. C7H7SO2Cl**: The database expects the strict ordering, not the way the formula is drawn.
- **All elements alphabetically, including C and H**: C and H come first regardless of the alphabet.
- **Heaviest element first, e.g. SClO2C7H7**: Mass order is not used.

*Source: Manual p.28.*

variants.stem: Which formula is in the order chemnetbase wants?
variants.explanation:
**C6H5Br for bromobenzene.** C, H, then Br alphabetically.

Why the others fail:
- **BrC6H5**: Br must not come first.
- **C6BrH5**: H comes immediately after C.
- **H5C6Br**: C comes first.

variants.explanation:
**SciFinder.** Chemical Abstracts (from 1907) was computerised; NTU subscribes to the version called SciFinder.

Why the others fail:
- **Scopus**: Scopus searches authors and topics and is not Chemical Abstracts.
- **Reaxys**: Reaxys is the Beilstein/Gmelin database, a different (German) service.

metadata.title: On a silica TLC plate, which of ferrocene, acetylferrocene and 1,1'...

variants.perspectiveLabel: TLC: Rf, polarity and visualising agents
variants.stem: On a silica TLC plate, which of ferrocene, acetylferrocene and 1,1'-diacetylferrocene has the highest Rf?
variants.explanation:
**Ferrocene.** It has no polar group, so it sticks least to silica and runs furthest; each added acetyl group makes the compound more polar and lowers Rf.

Why the others fail:
- **Acetylferrocene**: It has one polar C=O, so it is more strongly held than ferrocene and runs lower.
- **1,1'-Diacetylferrocene**: Two carbonyl groups make it the most polar of the three, so it has the lowest Rf.
- **All three have the same Rf because they share the ferrocene core**: Rf depends on overall polarity, and the acetyl groups change it a lot.

*Source: Manual p.24.*

options.label: Ferrocene
Acetylferrocene
1,1'-Diacetylferrocene
All three have the same Rf because they share the ferrocene core

variants.perspectiveLabel: TLC: Rf, polarity and visualising agents
variants.stem: A TLC plate shows two spots, one at Rf 0.65 and one at Rf 0.20. Which statement is correct?
variants.explanation:
**The Rf 0.20 compound is the more polar one.** The more polar a compound, the lower its Rf, because it is held more strongly by the silica.

Why the others fail:
- **The Rf 0.65 compound is the more polar one**: This reverses the relationship: a higher Rf means a less polar compound.
- **The Rf 0.20 compound is smaller in molecular mass**: Rf is governed by polarity, not molecular mass.
- **Polarity cannot be inferred from Rf at all**: On a given plate and solvent, Rf ranks polarity.

*Source: Manual p.24.*

options.label: The Rf 0.20 compound is the more polar one
The Rf 0.65 compound is the more polar one
The Rf 0.20 compound is smaller in molecular mass
Polarity cannot be inferred from Rf at all

metadata.title: Why are ionic compounds almost never analysed by TLC?

variants.perspectiveLabel: TLC: Rf, polarity and visualising agents
variants.stem: Why are ionic compounds almost never analysed by TLC?
variants.explanation:
**They are so polar that they hardly move from the baseline.** Very polar compounds have Rf near zero, so the plate tells you nothing.

Why the others fail:
- **They dissolve in the mobile phase and run with the solvent front**: It is the opposite: they stick to the silica and stay at the origin.
- **They decompose on silica to give neutral products**: The manual gives high polarity, not decomposition, as the reason.
- **They cannot be seen by any visualising agent**: Visualisation is a separate issue; the problem is that they do not move.

*Source: Manual p.24.*

options.label: They are so polar that they hardly move from the baseline
They dissolve in the mobile phase and run with the solvent front
They decompose on silica to give neutral products
They cannot be seen by any visualising agent

metadata.title: In first-year labs every spot showed under UV light. What does the ...

variants.perspectiveLabel: TLC: Rf, polarity and visualising agents
variants.stem: In first-year labs every spot showed under UV light. What does the manual warn about CM2061?
variants.explanation:
**Not every compound is visible under UV, so other visualising agents may be needed.** Compounds without a chromophore (for example alkenes and simple alcohols) can be invisible under UV and need a stain.

Why the others fail:
- **UV light can no longer be used in the teaching lab**: UV is still used; the warning is that it will not show everything.
- **All spots now need iodine because UV damages silica**: Nothing says UV damages the plate; iodine is one optional stain.
- **Only coloured compounds can be analysed by TLC**: Colourless compounds are analysed routinely; the point is to pick the right visualisation.

*Source: Manual p.24.*

options.label: Not every compound is visible under UV, so other visualising agents may be needed
UV light can no longer be used in the teaching lab
All spots now need iodine because UV damages silica
Only coloured compounds can be analysed by TLC

metadata.title: A TLC spot is an alcohol with no chromophore. Which visualising age...

variants.perspectiveLabel: TLC: Rf, polarity and visualising agents
variants.stem: A TLC spot is an alcohol with no chromophore. Which visualising agent does the manual recommend for alcohols, silyl ethers and epoxides?
variants.explanation:
**Acidic ammonium molybdate, dipped and heated above 100 °C, giving dark blue spots.** This is the manual's agent for alcohols and related compounds.

Why the others fail:
- **2,4-Dinitrophenylhydrazine, giving yellow to red spots**: DNP targets aldehydes and ketones, not alcohols.
- **Potassium permanganate, giving yellow spots on purple**: Permanganate is listed for alkenes and alkynes.
- **Iodine alone, which is specific to alcohols**: Iodine gives dark brown spots with many compounds and is not specific to alcohols.

*Source: Manual p.24.*

options.label: Acidic ammonium molybdate, dipped and heated above 100 °C, giving dark blue spots
2,4-Dinitrophenylhydrazine, giving yellow to red spots
Potassium permanganate, giving yellow spots on purple
Iodine alone, which is specific to alcohols

variants.perspectiveLabel: TLC: Rf, polarity and visualising agents
variants.stem: Which stain is the best choice to reveal an aryl ketone or an aldehyde, giving yellow, orange or red spots?
variants.explanation:
**2,4-Dinitrophenylhydrazine (DNP).** DNP is recommended for aldehydes and ketones, especially conjugated or aryl; usually no heating is needed.

Why the others fail:
- **Acidic ammonium molybdate**: That one is for alcohols, silyl ethers and epoxides, and needs heating.
- **Potassium permanganate**: Permanganate is chosen for unsaturated C=C and C≡C.
- **Iodine vapour**: It stains many compound types brown but is not the carbonyl-specific stain.

*Source: Manual p.24.*

options.label: 2,4-Dinitrophenylhydrazine (DNP)
Acidic ammonium molybdate
Potassium permanganate
Iodine vapour

variants.perspectiveLabel: TLC: Rf, polarity and visualising agents
variants.stem: A compound containing only a C=C double bond and no chromophore is run on TLC. Which stain shows it as a yellow spot on a purple background?
variants.explanation:
**Potassium permanganate (dip; usually no heating).** Permanganate oxidises alkenes and alkynes, leaving a yellow spot where the purple reagent was consumed.

Why the others fail:
- **Acidic ammonium molybdate**: It is for alcohols and similar oxygen compounds and gives dark blue spots.
- **2,4-Dinitrophenylhydrazine**: It reacts with C=O groups, not with an isolated C=C.
- **No stain: all organic compounds show under UV**: An isolated alkene has no UV chromophore at the usual wavelength.

*Source: Manual p.24.*

options.label: Potassium permanganate (dip; usually no heating)
Acidic ammonium molybdate
2,4-Dinitrophenylhydrazine
No stain: all organic compounds show under UV

variants.perspectiveLabel: TLC: Rf, polarity and visualising agents
variants.stem: After developing a plate with iodine, you want to visualise it a second way. Is that possible?
variants.explanation:
**Yes, once the iodine has evaporated another method can be used.** The manual notes that iodine staining is reversible, so the plate can then be stained with another agent.

Why the others fail:
- **No, iodine permanently ruins the silica**: The manual states the plate can be visualised by another method after the I₂ evaporates.
- **Yes, but only with UV light**: Any other method may be used; UV is not the only choice.
- **No, because iodine reacts with every spot irreversibly**: The brown spots fade as the iodine leaves the plate.

*Source: Manual p.24.*

options.label: Yes, once the iodine has evaporated another method can be used
No, iodine permanently ruins the silica
Yes, but only with UV light
No, because iodine reacts with every spot irreversibly

metadata.title: In which direction should cooling water pass through a reflux conde...

variants.stem: In which direction should cooling water pass through a reflux condenser?
variants.explanation:
**In at the bottom and out at the top.** The jacket then fills completely and the coolest water meets the hot vapour where it matters.

Why the others fail:
- **In at the top and out at the bottom**: The jacket would not fill properly, leaving air pockets and poor cooling.
- **Either way, it makes no difference**: The manual specifies bottom in, top out.
- **No water at all; air cooling is sufficient**: Only special cases (such as 200 °C heating in Expt 8 or the acetylation in Expt 7) use an air condenser.

*Source: Manual p.24.*

options.label: In at the bottom and out at the top
In at the top and out at the bottom
Either way, it makes no difference
No water at all; air cooling is sufficient

metadata.title: Where should a reflux apparatus be clamped?

variants.stem: Where should a reflux apparatus be clamped?
variants.explanation:
**At the neck of the flask.** The flask neck supports the whole assembly; the manual warns against clamping the condenser and relying on a plastic clip to hold the flask.

Why the others fail:
- **On the condenser, with a plastic clip holding the flask**: The manual says never to do this, even if a TA suggests it.
- **On the top of the condenser only**: That leaves the flask supported by the joint alone.
- **Anywhere, provided the clamp is tight**: The neck of the flask is the stated position.

*Source: Manual p.24; 2015 paper style.*

options.label: At the neck of the flask
On the condenser, with a plastic clip holding the flask
On the top of the condenser only
Anywhere, provided the clamp is tight

metadata.title: For which solvent is ice-water (rather than tap water) needed in th...

variants.stem: For which solvent is ice-water (rather than tap water) needed in the condenser when heating under reflux?
variants.explanation:
**Diethyl ether.** Its boiling point is very low, so ordinary water may not condense all the vapour.

Why the others fail:
- **Toluene**: Its boiling point is well above room temperature; ordinary tap water condenses it.
- **Ethanol**: It boils at about 78 °C, so ordinary cooling water is enough.
- **Tetrahydrofuran**: It boils near 66 °C, still high enough for tap water.

*Source: Manual p.25; 2015 paper style.*

options.label: Diethyl ether
Toluene
Ethanol
Tetrahydrofuran

metadata.title: Which statement about heating a reflux is correct?

variants.stem: Which statement about heating a reflux is correct?
variants.explanation:
**Use an oil bath, not direct heating, with the oil level below the liquid level in the flask, and add a stir bar or anti-bumping granules.** These are the manual's instructions: the oil level should be below the level of the liquid.

Why the others fail:
- **Heat the flask directly on the hotplate to save time**: The manual says to use an oil bath (not direct heating).
- **Keep the oil level above the liquid so the heating is more even**: The diagram specifies the oil below the liquid level.
- **No stir bar is needed once the solvent is boiling**: A stir bar or anti-bumping granules is required to prevent bumping.

*Source: Manual pp.24-25.*

options.label: Use an oil bath, not direct heating, with the oil level below the liquid level in the flask, and add a stir bar or anti-bumping granules
Heat the flask directly on the hotplate to save time
Keep the oil level above the liquid so the heating is more even
No stir bar is needed once the solvent is boiling

metadata.title: Why do chemists heat a reaction at the boiling point of the solvent...

variants.stem: Why do chemists heat a reaction at the boiling point of the solvent under reflux?
variants.explanation:
**The temperature stays constant at the solvent's boiling point, while the condenser returns the vapour to the flask.** A boiling liquid cannot exceed its boiling point, and the condenser stops the solvent from escaping.

Why the others fail:
- **To distil off the product continuously**: Reflux returns the vapour; it does not collect it.
- **To raise the temperature above the boiling point**: A liquid at atmospheric pressure cannot be heated above its boiling point.
- **To remove water from the system**: Nothing in reflux removes water; it just holds the temperature.

*Source: Manual p.24.*

options.label: The temperature stays constant at the solvent's boiling point, while the condenser returns the vapour to the flask
To distil off the product continuously
To raise the temperature above the boiling point
To remove water from the system

metadata.title: Why is the flask on a rotary evaporator rotated rapidly?

variants.stem: Why is the flask on a rotary evaporator rotated rapidly?
variants.explanation:
**To ensure smooth boiling; no rotation or slow rotation gives bumping.** The manual says rotate rapidly (not slowly) for this reason.

Why the others fail:
- **To spin the water out of the sample by centrifugal force**: Rotation promotes smooth, even evaporation; it is not a centrifuge.
- **To keep the bath temperature constant**: The bath has its own control; do not adjust its setting.
- **To increase the pressure in the flask**: The pump lowers the pressure; rotation does not change it.

*Source: Manual p.25.*

options.label: To ensure smooth boiling; no rotation or slow rotation gives bumping
To spin the water out of the sample by centrifugal force
To keep the bath temperature constant
To increase the pressure in the flask

metadata.title: Which set of rotary-evaporator instructions matches the manual?

variants.stem: Which set of rotary-evaporator instructions matches the manual?
variants.explanation:
**Bath at 35-40 °C (do not adjust it), rotate rapidly, flask less than half full.** These are the three points on pp.25 and 46.

Why the others fail:
- **Bath at 80 °C to be quick, rotate slowly, flask completely full**: All three are wrong: bumping and overfilling are the typical accidents.
- **Bath at 35-40 °C, rotate slowly, flask half full or more**: Slow rotation bumps, and the flask must be less than half full.
- **Bath at room temperature, no rotation, flask two-thirds full**: No rotation causes bumping and an overfilled flask will bump into the condenser.

*Source: Manual pp.25, 46.*

options.label: Bath at 35-40 °C (do not adjust it), rotate rapidly, flask less than half full
Bath at 80 °C to be quick, rotate slowly, flask completely full
Bath at 35-40 °C, rotate slowly, flask half full or more
Bath at room temperature, no rotation, flask two-thirds full

metadata.title: What makes solvents evaporate so easily on a rotary evaporator?

variants.stem: What makes solvents evaporate so easily on a rotary evaporator?
variants.explanation:
**The pump holds the sample under low pressure, so the solvent boils at a low temperature.** The vapour then condenses in the cooled condenser and drops into the collecting flask.

Why the others fail:
- **The very hot bath boils the solvent off**: The bath is only 35-40 °C; it is the low pressure that makes boiling easy.
- **The condenser pulls the vapour out chemically**: It simply cools the vapour back to liquid.
- **Fast rotation throws the liquid out of the flask**: Rotation ensures smooth boiling; it does not eject liquid.

*Source: Manual p.25.*

options.label: The pump holds the sample under low pressure, so the solvent boils at a low temperature
The very hot bath boils the solvent off
The condenser pulls the vapour out chemically
Fast rotation throws the liquid out of the flask

metadata.title: How does column chromatography differ from TLC in the way the solve...

variants.stem: How does column chromatography differ from TLC in the way the solvent moves?
variants.explanation:
**On TLC the solvent moves up the plate; in a column it flows down through the silica.** Both rely on the same principle (polarity); the column is preparative and collects fractions.

Why the others fail:
- **On TLC it moves down and in the column up**: This is reversed.
- **Both move the solvent upwards**: Column solvent runs downwards.
- **The solvent does not move on a column; the silica does**: The solvent flows through the stationary silica.

*Source: Manual p.44.*

options.label: On TLC the solvent moves up the plate; in a column it flows down through the silica
On TLC it moves down and in the column up
Both move the solvent upwards
The solvent does not move on a column; the silica does

metadata.title: Why must the silica never be allowed to run dry?

variants.stem: Why must the silica never be allowed to run dry?
variants.explanation:
**Air gets in, the packing cracks and the separation is spoiled.** Good packing means good separation; once the solvent level drops below the top of the silica, channels open up. Take the pump off as the hexane reaches the top of the silica. *(Beyond the manual: standard organic or analytical chemistry.)*

Why the others fail:
- **The silica would catch fire**: There is no fire hazard; the problem is the separation.
- **The coloured bands would turn white**: The bands keep their colours; the problem is channelling.
- **The stopcock would seize**: That is unrelated to the packing.

*Source: Manual p.45.*

options.label: Air gets in, the packing cracks and the separation is spoiled
The silica would catch fire
The coloured bands would turn white
The stopcock would seize

metadata.title: In Expt 7, which compound comes off the column first with hexane?

variants.stem: In Expt 7, which compound comes off the column first with hexane?
variants.explanation:
**Unreacted ferrocene, the least polar component.** Less polar compounds spend less time on the silica, so they elute first; acetylferrocene needs a more polar eluent.

Why the others fail:
- **Acetylferrocene**: It is more polar than ferrocene (one carbonyl), so it moves more slowly.
- **Diacetylferrocene**: It is the most polar of the three and elutes last.
- **All three together, since they are coloured**: Colour plays no part in the separation; polarity does.

*Source: Manual pp.43, 46.*

options.label: Unreacted ferrocene, the least polar component
Acetylferrocene
Diacetylferrocene
All three together, since they are coloured

metadata.title: After the first orange fraction has come off with hexane, why is th...

variants.stem: After the first orange fraction has come off with hexane, why is the eluent changed to 4:1 hexane:ethyl acetate?
variants.explanation:
**The second band is more polar and needs a more polar eluent to move down the column.** Ethyl acetate raises the eluent polarity, so the more strongly held compound can be eluted.

Why the others fail:
- **The first band must be washed off the silica with ethyl acetate**: The first band has already eluted; the change is to move the next one.
- **Hexane has run out and any solvent will do**: The manual specifies a particular, more polar mixture.
- **Ethyl acetate stops the second band from decomposing**: The purpose is polarity, not stabilisation.

*Source: Manual p.46.*

options.label: The second band is more polar and needs a more polar eluent to move down the column
The first band must be washed off the silica with ethyl acetate
Hexane has run out and any solvent will do
Ethyl acetate stops the second band from decomposing

metadata.title: Which statement about packing the column is consistent with the man...

variants.stem: Which statement about packing the column is consistent with the manual?
variants.explanation:
**Use just enough sand to cover the cotton wool, and do not pack the cotton wool too tightly or the flow will be too slow.** Both points are on the diagrams; a clean joint at the top is also essential.

Why the others fail:
- **Pack the cotton wool as tightly as possible so no silica escapes**: The manual warns that a tight plug makes the flow too slow.
- **Fill the column with dry silica first, then add hexane from above**: The silica is made into a slurry in hexane and poured in so all the air is expelled.
- **Leave silica on the ground-glass joint for a better seal**: The joint must be entirely free of silica so the air-pump adapter seals properly.

*Source: Manual pp.44-45.*

options.label: Use just enough sand to cover the cotton wool, and do not pack the cotton wool too tightly or the flow will be too slow
Pack the cotton wool as tightly as possible so no silica escapes
Fill the column with dry silica first, then add hexane from above
Leave silica on the ground-glass joint for a better seal

metadata.title: Why is the crude product dissolved in only 1-2 mL of toluene before...

variants.stem: Why is the crude product dissolved in only 1-2 mL of toluene before loading it on the column?
variants.explanation:
**A small volume applies the sample as a narrow band, giving a cleaner separation.** A wide starting band would overlap with the next band. *(Beyond the manual: standard organic or analytical chemistry.)*

Why the others fail:
- **Toluene is the eluent and must be used in a large volume**: The eluent is hexane (then hexane:ethyl acetate); toluene is only used to load the sample.
- **Toluene reacts with silica to fix the sample**: It just dissolves the sample for loading.
- **More toluene would make the silica dry**: The reason is band width, not drying.

*Source: Manual p.45.*

options.label: A small volume applies the sample as a narrow band, giving a cleaner separation
Toluene is the eluent and must be used in a large volume
Toluene reacts with silica to fix the sample
More toluene would make the silica dry

metadata.title: What do you do with the test-tube fractions from the column?

variants.stem: What do you do with the test-tube fractions from the column?
variants.explanation:
**Check them by TLC against authentic ferrocene, combine tubes with identical components, then evaporate on the rotavap in a less-than-half-full pre-weighed flask.** This is how pure fractions are identified and recovered.

Why the others fail:
- **Combine all the tubes, since the bands are already separated**: Each tube may hold a different component; TLC tells you which to combine.
- **Evaporate each tube separately on a hotplate**: Identical fractions are combined and evaporated on the rotavap.
- **Discard every tube that is not orange**: Colourless fractions may still contain product; TLC decides.

*Source: Manual pp.44, 46.*

options.label: Check them by TLC against authentic ferrocene, combine tubes with identical components, then evaporate on the rotavap in a less-than-half-full pre-weighed flask
Combine all the tubes, since the bands are already separated
Evaporate each tube separately on a hotplate
Discard every tube that is not orange

metadata.title: Why does flash chromatography use an air pump on the top of the col...

variants.stem: Why does flash chromatography use an air pump on the top of the column?
variants.explanation:
**Very fine silica gives better resolution but flows too slowly by gravity, so gentle air pressure pushes the solvent through.** The manual notes aquarium pumps provide the small pressure needed.

Why the others fail:
- **To dry the silica before use**: Never let the silica go dry; the pressure is applied to the solvent.
- **To evaporate the eluent as it descends**: The pump pushes the liquid through; it does not evaporate it.
- **To keep air out of the column**: The reverse: pressure drives solvent, not an inert atmosphere.

*Source: Manual p.44.*

To dry the silica before use
To evaporate the eluent as it descends
To keep air out of the column

metadata.title: In Expt 5E, why is the crude product sublimed under vacuum (about 6...

variants.stem: In Expt 5E, why is the crude product sublimed under vacuum (about 6 mmHg) with gentle heating of at most 50 °C?
variants.explanation:
**The solid passes into vapour at low temperature under reduced pressure and re-forms on the cold surface, leaving non-volatile impurities behind.** Reduced pressure lets a sublimation happen without melting or decomposing the product.

Why the others fail:
- **The vacuum removes the solvent from the crude solid**: Solvent was removed on the rotavap before; sublimation separates by volatility.
- **The cold water jacket is there to crystallise the product from solution**: Nothing is in solution; the vapour deposits directly as a solid on the cold finger.
- **Heating above 50 °C would be fine but is slower**: The manual caps the temperature at 50 °C; hotter heating risks melting or decomposition.

*Source: Manual p.39.*

variants.stem: Put the sublimation shut-down steps in the order the manual gives them.
variants.explanation:
Stop heating, then stop the cooling water, then release the vacuum, and only then take the apparatus apart to scrape the sublimed solid from the cone.

metadata.title: Which preparation of the sublimation apparatus is correct?

variants.stem: Which preparation of the sublimation apparatus is correct?
variants.explanation:
**Grease the joint, fit the top, connect the vertical tube to the pump and pass ice-cold water through the cooling jacket before applying vacuum and heating.** A greased joint holds the vacuum and the ice-cold finger traps the vapour.

Why the others fail:
- **Leave the joint ungreased so the apparatus can be opened quickly**: The joint is greased to hold the vacuum.
- **Heat first, then connect the vacuum when the solid melts**: The solid is sublimed under vacuum with gentle heating, not melted.
- **Pass hot water through the jacket to prevent condensation**: The finger is cooled with ice-cold water so the vapour deposits on it.

*Source: Manual p.39.*

metadata.title: Which course technique tells you whether a chiral product is racemi...

variants.stem: Which course technique tells you whether a chiral product is racemic or enriched in one enantiomer?
variants.explanation:
**Polarimetry, because only a non-racemic sample rotates plane-polarised light.** Most other properties and spectra are identical for racemate and non-racemate; optical rotation is what differs.

Why the others fail:
- **Melting point of the product alone**: Enantiomers have identical melting points, and a racemate's may or may not differ, so mp does not reliably give the enantiomer ratio.
- **1H NMR**: In an achiral solvent the spectra of enantiomers and of a racemate are identical.
- **IR spectroscopy**: IR spectra of enantiomers are identical too.

*Source: Manual pp.40, 42; 2015 paper style.*

options.label: Polarimetry, because only a non-racemic sample rotates plane-polarised light

1H NMR
IR spectroscopy

metadata.title: Which items must be stated when reporting a specific rotation [α]D?

variants.stem: Which items must be stated when reporting a specific rotation [α]D?
variants.explanation:
**The wavelength (sodium D line), temperature, solvent and concentration.** The rotation varies with all of these, so a value without them cannot be compared.

Why the others fail:
- **Only the sign of the rotation**: The magnitude and conditions matter.
- **Only the concentration**: Temperature, wavelength and solvent also change the value.
- **The melting point of the sample**: It is not part of the rotation report.

*Source: Manual p.42.*

options.label: The wavelength (sodium D line), temperature, solvent and concentration
Only the sign of the rotation
Only the concentration

metadata.title: How is a sample prepared for polarimetry in Expt 6?

variants.stem: How is a sample prepared for polarimetry in Expt 6?
variants.explanation:
**Weigh 50-100 mg accurately into a 5 or 10 mL volumetric flask, make up to the mark with CH₂Cl₂, and fill the cell with no trapped bubbles.** An accurately known concentration is needed to calculate [α], and bubbles disturb the light path.

Why the others fail:
- **Dissolve an approximate amount in any volume of water**: The concentration must be known accurately, so a volumetric flask and a stated solvent (CH₂Cl₂) are used.
- **Put the neat solid straight into the cell**: The measurement needs a solution of known concentration.
- **Use any flask, since concentration does not affect rotation**: The rotation is proportional to concentration and path length.

*Source: Manual p.42.*

- **A TA, because the lamp is dangerous UV**: The stated reason is the cost of the cells.
- **The lab technician, because the sample is hazardous**: The stated requirement is a TA, for the cell expense.

metadata.title: Which instrument would you use to find the number of unpaired elect...

variants.stem: Which instrument would you use to find the number of unpaired electrons in a metal complex?
variants.explanation:
**A magnetic susceptibility balance.** It measures susceptibility, from which the effective magnetic moment and the number of unpaired electrons follow. *(Beyond the manual: standard organic or analytical chemistry.)*

Why the others fail:
- **A polarimeter**: It measures optical rotation of chiral compounds.
- **An NMR spectrometer recording a routine proton spectrum**: A routine spectrum does not count unpaired electrons (paramagnetism in fact broadens signals); special methods such as the Evans method are a different measurement and are not what the course uses.
- **An IR spectrometer**: It identifies functional groups by vibrations.

*Source: Manual p.4 (mentioned); 2015 paper style.*

options.label: A magnetic susceptibility balance
A polarimeter
An NMR spectrometer recording a routine proton spectrum
An IR spectrometer

metadata.title: The complex Py₂Zn(NCO)₂ from Expt 1D has zinc(II), a d¹⁰ ion. What ...

variants.stem: The complex Py₂Zn(NCO)₂ from Expt 1D has zinc(II), a d¹⁰ ion. What would a magnetic susceptibility measurement show?
variants.explanation:
**Diamagnetic: no unpaired electrons.** A filled d subshell has no unpaired electrons, so the sample is repelled weakly by a magnetic field. *(Beyond the manual: standard organic or analytical chemistry.)*

Why the others fail:
- **Paramagnetic with two unpaired electrons**: Two unpaired electrons would need a d⁸ or d²-type configuration, not d¹⁰.
- **Paramagnetic with one unpaired electron**: Zn²⁺ has a full 3d subshell.
- **Ferromagnetic**: Ferromagnetism requires cooperative ordering in solids like iron.

*Source: Manual p.32; CM2021 magnetism.*

options.label: Diamagnetic: no unpaired electrons
Paramagnetic with two unpaired electrons
Paramagnetic with one unpaired electron
Ferromagnetic

metadata.title: Why would a chemist remove formic acid by distillation under reduce...

variants.stem: Why would a chemist remove formic acid by distillation under reduced pressure instead of at atmospheric pressure?
variants.explanation:
**The boiling point drops with pressure, so the acid distils at a lower temperature and the sensitive product is not overheated.** Lowering the pressure is a way to distil without excessive heat. *(Beyond the manual: standard organic or analytical chemistry.)*

Why the others fail:
- **Reduced pressure raises the boiling point so the acid stays in the flask**: It lowers the boiling point.
- **Reduced pressure makes the acid react with the vacuum pump oil**: Nothing of the kind is the aim.
- **It is the only way to separate a liquid from a solid**: Filtration does that; distillation is chosen to avoid high temperatures.

*Source: Manual p.4 (video); 2015 paper style.*

Reduced pressure makes the acid react with the vacuum pump oil

metadata.title: The boiling point of formic acid is 101 °C at atmospheric pressure....

variants.stem: The boiling point of formic acid is 101 °C at atmospheric pressure. Using a pressure-temperature nomograph, roughly what would it boil at under 180 mmHg?
variants.explanation:
**About 60 °C.** A straight edge through 101 °C on the 760 mmHg scale and 180 mmHg on the pressure scale reads about 60 °C: the boiling point falls by roughly 40 °C when the pressure drops to about a quarter of atmospheric. (A check from vapour-pressure data, about 44 mmHg at 25 °C for formic acid, gives about 58 °C.) *(Beyond the manual: standard organic or analytical chemistry.)*

Why the others fail:
- **About 100 °C**: That would mean pressure has no effect; boiling points fall substantially at 180 mmHg.
- **About 80 °C**: A drop of only about 20 °C is too small for a reduction to one quarter of atmospheric pressure.
- **About 40 °C**: This over-reads the drop: 40 °C would need a pressure well below 180 mmHg (about 100 mmHg for this acid).
- **About 5 °C**: Far too low; the acid freezes at about 8 °C and would not boil there.

*Source: 2015 paper style; Year-1 technique (nomograph).*

options.label: About 60 °C
About 100 °C
About 80 °C
About 40 °C
About 5 °C

metadata.title: A nomograph has three scales: observed boiling point, boiling point...

variants.stem: A nomograph has three scales: observed boiling point, boiling point corrected to 760 mmHg and pressure. How is it used?
variants.explanation:
**Lay a straight edge across two known values; the line meets the third scale at the value you need.** Any two of the three quantities fix the third. *(Beyond the manual: standard organic or analytical chemistry.)*

Why the others fail:
- **Read each scale separately and add the values**: The scales are linked by a straight line, not added.
- **Multiply the pressure by the boiling point**: No such calculation is used.
- **Use only the pressure scale, since boiling points never change**: The whole point is how boiling point changes with pressure.

*Source: Year-1 technique (nomograph).*

options.label: Lay a straight edge across two known values; the line meets the third scale at the value you need

Use only the pressure scale, since boiling points never change

metadata.title: What is an azeotrope?

variants.stem: What is an azeotrope?
variants.explanation:
**A mixture of liquids that boils at a constant temperature with the vapour having the same composition as the liquid, so simple distillation cannot separate it further.** It behaves like a single compound with its own boiling point. *(Beyond the manual: standard organic or analytical chemistry.)*

Why the others fail:
- **A mixture that boils over a very wide temperature range**: That describes an ordinary mixture; an azeotrope boils at one temperature.
- **A solid that sublimes without melting**: That is sublimation, unrelated to azeotropes.
- **Any liquid that cannot be distilled**: Most liquids distil; an azeotrope limits the separation of a particular mixture.

*Source: 2015 paper style; Year-1 technique.*

options.label: A mixture of liquids that boils at a constant temperature with the vapour having the same composition as the liquid, so simple distillation cannot separate it further
A mixture that boils over a very wide temperature range
A solid that sublimes without melting
Any liquid that cannot be distilled

metadata.title: Formic acid (bp 101 °C) and water form a maximum-boiling azeotrope ...
metadata.source: 2015 paper style; CRC Handbook azeotrope data

variants.stem: Formic acid (bp 101 °C) and water form a maximum-boiling azeotrope (about 107 °C, roughly 77 wt% acid). How does water in the flask affect the distillation of formic acid?
variants.explanation:
**The acid-water azeotrope distils at a higher temperature than pure formic acid, so water makes complete removal of the acid by simple distillation harder.** A maximum-boiling azeotrope holds the last of the acid back in the pot as a constant-boiling mixture; azeotropes do not always lower the boiling point. *(Beyond the manual: standard organic or analytical chemistry.)*

Why the others fail:
- **The mixture distils at a lower temperature, as ethanol-water does**: Ethanol-water is a minimum-boiling azeotrope, but formic acid-water is a maximum-boiling one.
- **Nothing changes: the acid distils at its normal 101 °C**: The azeotrope has its own, higher, boiling point.
- **Vigorous stirring breaks the azeotrope**: Stirring only prevents bumping; it does not change vapour-liquid equilibrium.

*Source: 2015 paper style; CRC Handbook azeotrope data.*

options.label: The acid-water azeotrope distils at a higher temperature than pure formic acid, so water makes complete removal of the acid by simple distillation harder

Nothing changes: the acid distils at its normal 101 °C
Vigorous stirring breaks the azeotrope

metadata.title: Which method prevents bumping during a distillation under reduced p...

variants.stem: Which method prevents bumping during a distillation under reduced pressure?
variants.explanation:
**Stir the liquid with a magnetic stir bar.** Boiling chips release trapped air at low pressure and stop working; a stir bar gives smooth boiling. *(Beyond the manual: standard organic or analytical chemistry.)*

Why the others fail:
- **Add fresh boiling chips (anti-bumping granules)**: Under vacuum the air in the granules is quickly lost, so they do not work.
- **Heat as strongly as possible to boil it off quickly**: Overheating increases the risk of bumping.
- **Open the system to air briefly during the distillation**: Opening the system defeats the reduced pressure.

*Source: Year-1 technique.*

metadata.title: Put the stages of a recrystallisation in a sensible order.

variants.stem: Put the stages of a recrystallisation in a sensible order.
variants.explanation:
Minimum hot solvent gives a saturated solution; slow cooling grows pure crystals; the ice bath maximises recovery; a little cold solvent washes the surface without dissolving the product. *(Beyond the manual: standard practice.)*

*Source: Manual pp.29, 34 (and Year-1 technique).*

Filter off any insoluble material while hot

metadata.title: What does the manual say happens if too much solvent is used in a r...

variants.stem: What does the manual say happens if too much solvent is used in a recrystallisation?
variants.explanation:
**The product will not crystallise on cooling, and the manual says the only way to recover it is by extraction.** This is a warning on p.29. (Beyond the manual: in practice, boiling off or rotavapping some of the solvent and cooling again also recovers the product.)

Why the others fail:
- **The crystals form faster and are purer**: The opposite: nothing crystallises if the solution is not saturated at the low temperature.
- **The product decomposes in the excess solvent**: Decomposition is not the issue; solubility is.
- **Nothing, because the product always crystallises on cooling**: It crystallises only from a saturated solution.

*Source: Manual p.29.*

options.label: The product will not crystallise on cooling, and the manual says the only way to recover it is by extraction

metadata.title: A recrystallisation from hot ethanol gave very poor recovery. Which

variants.stem: A recrystallisation from hot ethanol gave very poor recovery. Which changes would be likely to help? Select all that apply.
variants.explanation:
**Correct:** Use less hot ethanol to dissolve the material (a smaller volume leaves less product in solution); Cool the solution to a lower temperature at the end (solubility falls as the temperature falls); Add a little water to the hot solution to make the product less soluble (a poor solvent for the product that is miscible with ethanol lowers its solubility).

Why the others fail:
- **Wash the crystals with a large volume of warm ethanol**: this redissolves the product and sends it into the filtrate
- **Filter the solution while it is still hot and discard the filtrate**: the product is still dissolved in the hot filtrate and is thrown away

*(Beyond the manual: standard chemistry.)*

*Source: 2015 paper style; Manual p.29.*

metadata.title: Why is the collected solid washed with only "a little cold" solvent...

variants.stem: Why is the collected solid washed with only "a little cold" solvent on the Buchner funnel?
variants.explanation:
**Cold solvent in a small volume rinses off mother liquor without dissolving much product.** Warm or large volumes would redissolve the crystals. *(Beyond the manual: standard organic or analytical chemistry.)*

Why the others fail:
- **Cold solvent reacts with the product to purify it**: The wash is a physical rinse.
- **Large volumes of cold solvent are always better because they are cold**: Even cold solvent dissolves some product; use as little as will do.
- **Hot solvent removes impurities better and only a little is needed**: Hot solvent would dissolve the product and ruin the yield.

*Source: Manual pp.29, 34.*

options.label: Cold solvent in a small volume rinses off mother liquor without dissolving much product

metadata.title: Why do the procedures for 2-iodobenzoic acid and benzoic acid say t...

variants.stem: Why do the procedures for 2-iodobenzoic acid and benzoic acid say to cool the hot solution slowly?
variants.explanation:
**Slow cooling gives larger, purer crystals that exclude impurities, whereas rapid cooling traps impurities in small crystals.** The slow growth lets molecules of the product, and not impurities, fit the lattice. *(Beyond the manual: standard organic or analytical chemistry.)*

Why the others fail:
- **Slow cooling increases the solubility of the product**: Solubility drops with temperature on cooling, which is why crystals form.
- **Rapid cooling would decompose the acid**: Decomposition is not the issue.
- **The precipitate dissolves faster at lower temperature**: Crystals form as the temperature falls; they do not dissolve.

*Source: Manual pp.38, 51 (cool slowly); Year-1 technique.*

options.label: Slow cooling gives larger, purer crystals that exclude impurities, whereas rapid cooling traps impurities in small crystals
Slow cooling increases the solubility of the product

metadata.source: Manual pp.39, 41, 47; densities from standard tables

variants.stem: In Expt 5E the product is in dichloromethane and is washed with water in a separatory funnel. Which layer is at the bottom?
variants.explanation:
**Dichloromethane (the organic layer), because it is denser than water.** Dichloromethane is about 1.33 g/mL; the aqueous layer floats on top. *(Beyond the manual: standard organic or analytical chemistry.)*

Why the others fail:
- **Water, because organic solvents always float**: Diethyl ether and hexane float; dichloromethane sinks.
- **The two mix and form one layer**: Dichloromethane and water are immiscible.
- **The layers cannot be told apart**: Density decides which is which.

*Source: Manual pp.39, 41, 47; densities from standard tables.*

metadata.source: Manual p.41; densities from standard tables

variants.stem: In the work-up of Expt 6 the aqueous mixture is extracted twice with diethyl ether. Where is the ether layer in the separatory funnel?
variants.explanation:
**On top, because diethyl ether is less dense than water.** Ether is about 0.71 g/mL. *(Beyond the manual: standard organic or analytical chemistry.)*

Why the others fail:
- **At the bottom, like dichloromethane**: Ether is lighter than water, unlike dichloromethane.
- **Dissolved evenly in the aqueous phase**: Ether and water form two layers (ether is only slightly soluble in water).
- **It evaporates immediately and no layer forms**: It remains as a liquid layer at room temperature.

*Source: Manual p.41; densities from standard tables.*
