metadata.title: Why are the combined ether layers washed with brine (saturated aque...

variants.stem: Why are the combined ether layers washed with brine (saturated aqueous NaCl) before drying in Expt 6?
variants.explanation:
**Brine pulls dissolved water out of the organic layer and lowers the solubility of the organic product in the aqueous phase, so less drying agent is needed and less product is lost.** This is the "salting-out" effect. *(Beyond the manual: standard organic or analytical chemistry.)*

Why the others fail:
- **Brine neutralises traces of acid**: It is neutral; neutralisation needs a base such as NaHCO₃.
- **Brine converts the ester into its sodium salt**: No reaction takes place.
- **Brine increases the volume so the layers separate more slowly**: The purpose is removing water, not slowing separation.

*Source: Manual p.41 (brine wash).*

metadata.title: In Expt 8 the combined organic layers are washed with sodium bicarb...

variants.stem: In Expt 8 the combined organic layers are washed with sodium bicarbonate solution. What is the purpose and what do you watch for?
variants.explanation:
**It neutralises the HCl formed in the hydrolysis; CO₂ is released, so vent the funnel.** HCl plus bicarbonate gives chloride, water and carbon dioxide gas. *(Beyond the manual: standard organic or analytical chemistry.)*

Why the others fail:
- **It dries the organic layer; nothing is released**: Bicarbonate solution is aqueous and does not dry anything; gas is released.
- **It converts the siloxane to a silanol**: It only neutralises acid.
- **It extracts the siloxane into the water layer**: The siloxane stays in the organic layer.

*Source: Manual p.47.*

metadata.title: Which statement about magnesium sulfate and sodium sulfate as dryin...
metadata.source: Manual pp.39, 41, 47; properties from standard tables

variants.stem: Which statement about magnesium sulfate and sodium sulfate as drying agents is correct?
variants.explanation:
**Magnesium sulfate dries faster (a fine powder with a high capacity) but must be filtered; sodium sulfate is slower and neutral.** Both are used in the manual: MgSO₄ in Expt 8 and the NaBH₄ reduction in Expt 6, Na₂SO₄ in Expts 5E and the yeast work-up. *(Beyond the manual: standard organic or analytical chemistry.)*

Why the others fail:
- **Sodium sulfate is faster than magnesium sulfate**: Sodium sulfate is the slower of the two.
- **Magnesium sulfate cannot be filtered off**: It is a fine powder that is filtered off.
- **Neither removes water; they only change the colour of the solution**: They take up water of hydration from the organic solution.

*Source: Manual pp.39, 41, 47; properties from standard tables.*

variants.explanation:
**Filter off the drying agent and evaporate the solvent.** The manual does exactly this: filter, then rotavap. *(Beyond the manual: standard organic or analytical chemistry.)*

Why the others fail:
- **Evaporate with the drying agent still in the flask**: The solid would contaminate the product.
- **Add water to dissolve the drying agent**: That would re-wet the solution.
- **Pour the solution into the next experiment as it is**: The solvent must be removed to isolate the product.

metadata.title: What does a drying tube on top of an addition funnel or condenser do?

variants.perspectiveLabel: Drying tubes, oven-dried glassware and the Schlenk line
variants.stem: What does a drying tube on top of an addition funnel or condenser do?
variants.explanation:
**It lets gas move in and out while keeping moist air out of the apparatus.** The system stays open (no pressure build-up) but atmospheric water is trapped by the desiccant in the tube.

Why the others fail:
- **It seals the apparatus completely so no gas can escape**: A sealed system would build up pressure; a drying tube is vented.
- **It supplies dry nitrogen to the flask**: Nitrogen comes from a manifold or balloon, not from a drying tube.
- **It condenses solvent vapour**: That is the job of the condenser.

*Source: Manual pp.39, 44.*

metadata.title: Why does Expt 5E use a dried flask, an oven-dried stir bar, anhydro...

variants.perspectiveLabel: Drying tubes, oven-dried glassware and the Schlenk line
variants.stem: Why does Expt 5E use a dried flask, an oven-dried stir bar, anhydrous dichloromethane and a drying tube?
variants.explanation:
**Trifluoroacetic anhydride is moisture-sensitive: water would hydrolyse it to trifluoroacetic acid and consume the reagent.** Keeping water out preserves the electrophile for the pyrrole. *(Beyond the manual: standard organic or analytical chemistry.)*

Why the others fail:
- **The pyrrole explodes on contact with water**: The sensitive reagent is the anhydride; water would waste it.
- **Water would turn the dichloromethane into chloroform**: It would not.
- **Dry apparatus prevents the product from sublimating early**: The drying has nothing to do with the later sublimation.

*Source: Manual p.39.*

metadata.title: How is glassware prepared for a Grignard reaction in Expt 9?

variants.perspectiveLabel: Drying tubes, oven-dried glassware and the Schlenk line
variants.stem: How is glassware prepared for a Grignard reaction in Expt 9?
variants.explanation:
**Dried in an oven at about 120 °C for an hour, assembled hot, put under vacuum at once, then flushed with nitrogen when cool.** Looking dry is not enough: a film of water clings to glass surfaces and would destroy the Grignard reagent.

Why the others fail:
- **Rinsed with acetone and air-dried for a minute**: Acetone leaves traces of water and is not oven-drying.
- **Washed with water and used straight away**: Water destroys a Grignard reagent.
- **Dried in an oven, then left open on the bench to cool**: It would pick up moisture from the air as it cools; it is assembled hot and put under vacuum.

*Source: Manual p.50.*

options.label: Dried in an oven at about 120 °C for an hour, assembled hot, put under vacuum at once, then flushed with nitrogen when cool
Rinsed with acetone and air-dried for a minute

metadata.title: What does the vacuum-nitrogen double manifold (Schlenk line) allow?

variants.perspectiveLabel: Drying tubes, oven-dried glassware and the Schlenk line
variants.stem: What does the vacuum-nitrogen double manifold (Schlenk line) allow?
variants.explanation:
**The apparatus can be evacuated and refilled with nitrogen, so reagents and solvents are kept free of air and moisture.** This is what the Grignard preparation needs.

Why the others fail:
- **It heats the flask to a precise temperature**: It is a gas and vacuum manifold, not a heater.
- **It distils the ether continuously**: Collecting dry ether is done with a demonstrator's help; the line just supplies vacuum and nitrogen.
- **It filters the reaction mixture**: No filtration happens on a Schlenk line.

*Source: Manual p.49.*

metadata.title: Why is a pressure-equalising addition funnel used in the Grignard a...

variants.perspectiveLabel: Flask size, necks and addition funnels
variants.stem: Why is a pressure-equalising addition funnel used in the Grignard apparatus of Expt 9?
variants.explanation:
**The liquid drips in even though the funnel is closed under nitrogen, because the pressure above and below the liquid is equal.** A plain funnel with the top closed would not drain; with the top open it would admit moist air.

Why the others fail:
- **It heats the bromobenzene as it is added**: It has no heating function.
- **It filters the bromobenzene**: It is only a dropping device.
- **It lets you add the solid magnesium without a stopper**: The magnesium is already in the flask.

*Source: Manual p.50.*

metadata.title: In the Expt 9 apparatus, what is attached to each neck of the two-n...

variants.perspectiveLabel: Flask size, necks and addition funnels
variants.stem: In the Expt 9 apparatus, what is attached to each neck of the two-neck round-bottom flask?
variants.explanation:
**One neck carries the reflux condenser (with a connection to the manifold) and the other the pressure-equalising addition funnel.** Each necessary item needs its own neck, and the flask holds the magnesium in ether.

Why the others fail:
- **A thermometer and a stopper**: No thermometer is used and the funnel needs a neck.
- **Two condensers**: Only one is needed, and the addition funnel must be fitted.
- **An addition funnel and a stirrer**: A magnetic stir bar is used and the condenser is needed for reflux.

*Source: Manual p.50.*

metadata.title: A reaction mixture will have a total volume of about 640 mL. A rule...

variants.perspectiveLabel: Flask size, necks and addition funnels
variants.stem: A reaction mixture will have a total volume of about 640 mL. A rule of thumb is to fill a flask no more than half full. What is the smallest standard flask that fits?
variants.explanation:
**2 L (since 640 mL needs a flask of at least 1.3 L).** Half full or less means the flask volume must be at least twice the mixture volume, and 2 L is the next standard size above 1.28 L. *(Beyond the manual: standard organic or analytical chemistry.)*

Why the others fail:
- **500 mL**: It is smaller than the mixture itself.
- **1 L**: The mixture would fill it to about two-thirds, more than half.
- **5 L**: It would work but is far larger than necessary; the smallest standard flask that satisfies the rule is asked for.

*Source: 2015 paper style; Year-1 technique.*

metadata.title: A reaction needs a dropwise addition of a reagent, a thermometer to...

variants.perspectiveLabel: Flask size, necks and addition funnels
variants.stem: A reaction needs a dropwise addition of a reagent, a thermometer to monitor the exotherm and magnetic stirring. Using plain necks only (no multi-port adapters), what is the minimum number of necks on the flask?
variants.explanation:
**Two: one for the addition funnel and one for the thermometer.** A magnetic stir bar needs no neck; every other item that must enter the flask needs its own. *(Beyond the manual: standard organic or analytical chemistry.)*

Why the others fail:
- **One, since only one reagent is added**: Two items cannot enter through one bare neck.
- **Three, because stirring needs a neck**: Magnetic stirring works through the flask wall, so no neck is needed.
- **Four, one for each of the items plus a condenser**: No condenser is needed in this scenario.

*Source: 2015 paper style; Year-1 technique.*

variants.perspectiveLabel: Flask size, necks and addition funnels
variants.stem: In Expts 1B, 1C and 8 a separatory funnel is clamped above the flask. What is it doing there?
variants.explanation:
**It serves as an addition funnel: the stopcock lets the reagent solution be added slowly and controllably.** Slow addition controls the exotherm (and, in Expt 8, the HCl evolution).

Why the others fail:
- **It separates the layers of the product during the reaction**: No layers are separated at this stage.
- **It filters the reaction as it runs**: It does not filter.
- **It keeps the reaction under nitrogen**: It has no inert-gas function here.

*Source: Manual pp.30, 31, 47.*

metadata.title: Solids are run in IR as a nujol mull. Which absorptions in your spe...

variants.perspectiveLabel: IR of solids: the nujol bands
variants.stem: Solids are run in IR as a nujol mull. Which absorptions in your spectrum come from the nujol itself and should be ignored?
variants.explanation:
**The C-H stretches near 2920 and 2850 cm⁻¹ and the C-H bends near 1460 and 1377 cm⁻¹.** Nujol is a mineral oil (long-chain alkanes), so these four strong bands appear in every mull spectrum.

Why the others fail:
- **A broad band at 3300 cm⁻¹ and a sharp band at 1700 cm⁻¹**: Those are O-H and C=O regions; nujol has no such groups, so any band there is your sample's.
- **Bands at 2250 and 1650 cm⁻¹**: Nujol, a saturated hydrocarbon, absorbs at neither.
- **The whole region from 4000 to 400 cm⁻¹**: Nujol absorbs in only a few places; the rest of the spectrum is available for the sample.

*Source: Manual p.15.*

metadata.title: A student's mull spectrum shows only strong bands at about 2920, 28...

variants.perspectiveLabel: IR of solids: the nujol bands
variants.stem: A student's mull spectrum shows only strong bands at about 2920, 2850, 1460 and 1377 cm⁻¹ and nothing else. What should they do?
variants.explanation:
**Re-record the spectrum with a better sample, because too much nujol (or too little sample) was used.** The manual says that seeing only the nujol peaks means you used too much nujol, and the spectrum must be recorded again.

Why the others fail:
- **Report the compound as a long-chain alkane**: The bands are the mulling oil, not the sample.
- **Print it and note that the sample has no functional groups**: A sample with no bands means the sample was not in the beam, not that it has no groups.
- **Subtract the bands and hand in a spectrum with a gap**: The spectrum must be re-recorded rather than edited.

*Source: Manual p.15.*

variants.stem: Your IR spectrum has peaks pointing up instead of down. What does the manual advise?
variants.explanation:
**Correct the problem first and then print it; do not waste paper on a spectrum that looks wrong.** Upward peaks (or only nujol bands) mean something is wrong with the measurement.

Why the others fail:
- **Print it anyway and explain it in the report**: The manual says not to print a wrong-looking spectrum.
- **Turn the page upside down and use it as it is**: The spectrum should be recorded correctly instead.
- **Ask the TA to draw the missing bands by hand**: Spectra must be real data.

*Source: Manual p.15.*

metadata.source: Year-1 IR correlation (standard tables); 2015 paper style

variants.perspectiveLabel: IR: group frequencies you must know
variants.stem: A product is a saturated carboxylic acid with long CH₂ chains and no C=C. In which of these regions would it NOT show a band?
variants.explanation:
**1620-1680 cm⁻¹ (C=C).** There is no C=C; the acid O-H (very broad, 2500-3300), C-H (2850-2960) and C=O (1700-1725) are all present. *(Beyond the manual: standard organic or analytical chemistry.)*

Why the others fail:
- **2500-3300 cm⁻¹ (broad O-H)**: The carboxylic acid O-H gives a very broad band here.
- **2850-2960 cm⁻¹ (C-H)**: All saturated chains show C-H stretches here.
- **1700-1725 cm⁻¹ (C=O)**: The acid C=O absorbs here.

*Source: Year-1 IR correlation (standard tables); 2015 paper style.*

options.label: 2500-3300 cm⁻¹ (broad O-H)

variants.perspectiveLabel: IR: group frequencies you must know
variants.stem: At which frequency would benzoic acid show its strong C=O stretch?
variants.explanation:
**About 1690 cm⁻¹.** Conjugation with the aromatic ring lowers the C=O frequency from about 1710-1725 cm⁻¹ (saturated acid dimer) to about 1685-1690 cm⁻¹. *(Beyond the manual: standard organic or analytical chemistry.)*

Why the others fail:
- **About 1740 cm⁻¹**: That is typical of a saturated ester; hydrogen-bonded acid dimers absorb lower, and conjugation lowers it further.
- **About 1715 cm⁻¹**: This is a saturated acid; conjugation lowers it further.
- **About 1600 cm⁻¹**: That is the aromatic C=C region, not the carbonyl.

*Source: Year-1 IR correlation (standard tables); 2015 paper style.*

options.label: About 1690 cm⁻¹

About 1715 cm⁻¹
About 1600 cm⁻¹

variants.stem: Which functional group gives a broad, strong absorption between about 2500 and 3300 cm⁻¹?
variants.explanation:
**A carboxylic acid O-H (hydrogen-bonded).** Acid dimers give a very broad band overlapping the C-H stretches. *(Beyond the manual: standard organic or analytical chemistry.)*

Why the others fail:
- **A ketone C=O**: That is a sharp band near 1715 cm⁻¹.
- **An alkene C=C**: It gives a weak band near 1650 cm⁻¹.
- **A nitro group**: It gives two strong bands near 1550 and 1350 cm⁻¹.

*Source: Year-1 IR correlation (standard tables); 2015 paper style.*

variants.explanation:
**About 1550 and 1350 cm⁻¹.** These are the asymmetric and symmetric N-O stretches; the databook gives 1555-1540 and 1385-1350 cm⁻¹ for nitro compounds. *(Beyond the manual: standard organic or analytical chemistry.)*

Why the others fail:
- **About 3300 and 1650 cm⁻¹**: These suggest N-H and an amide C=O.
- **About 2250 and 2100 cm⁻¹**: Triple-bond region (nitrile, alkyne).
- **About 1740 and 1250 cm⁻¹**: These suggest an ester (C=O and C-O).

variants.perspectiveLabel: IR: group frequencies you must know
variants.stem: Which IR feature distinguishes a ketone from an alcohol most simply?
variants.explanation:
**A strong sharp C=O band near 1715 cm⁻¹ with no broad O-H band near 3300 cm⁻¹.** The alcohol shows the reverse: a broad O-H and no C=O. *(Beyond the manual: standard organic or analytical chemistry.)*

Why the others fail:
- **A band at 2900 cm⁻¹**: Both have C-H stretches.
- **A band at 1600 cm⁻¹ only**: That is the aromatic ring region and not specific to either.
- **Neither can be distinguished by IR**: IR separates them clearly.

*Source: Year-1 IR correlation (standard tables); 2015 paper style.*

variants.perspectiveLabel: IR: group frequencies you must know
variants.stem: Conjugating a ketone C=O to a C=C or an aryl ring changes its IR stretch how?
variants.explanation:
**It lowers the frequency, to about 1685-1660 cm⁻¹ (databook, α,β-unsaturated ketones) compared with 1725-1705 cm⁻¹ for a saturated ketone.** Delocalisation weakens the C=O bond, as seen for dibenzalacetone and acylferrocenes. *(Beyond the manual: standard organic or analytical chemistry.)*

Why the others fail:
- **It raises it to about 1750 cm⁻¹**: Raising occurs for strained rings and esters, not conjugation.
- **It does not change it**: Conjugation lowers it by 30-60 cm⁻¹.
- **It makes the band disappear**: The band stays strong.

*Source: Year-1 IR correlation (standard tables); 2015 paper style.*

metadata.title: The raw data from the NMR spectrometer is a free induction decay (F...

variants.stem: The raw data from the NMR spectrometer is a free induction decay (FID). What is on its x-axis, and what turns it into a spectrum?
variants.explanation:
**Time; a Fourier transform converts it into a spectrum with chemical shift on the x-axis.** The FID is a time-domain signal; the transform gives the frequency-domain spectrum.

Why the others fail:
- **Chemical shift; a baseline correction is all it needs**: The FID has time, not shift, on the axis.
- **Frequency in Hz; integration turns it into a spectrum**: Integration measures peak areas; the Fourier transform is the conversion.
- **Temperature; a calibration curve converts it**: No temperature axis is involved.

*Source: Manual p.16.*

metadata.title: What must be submitted with a lab report for an NMR spectrum?

variants.stem: What must be submitted with a lab report for an NMR spectrum?
variants.explanation:
**The spectrum limited to the normal range (0-10 or 0-8 ppm) and expansions of the peaks of interest to show splitting.** Expansions are needed whenever splitting patterns must be examined.

Why the others fail:
- **Only the raw FID**: The FID is unprocessed; the processed spectrum is required.
- **Only a table of shifts, without the spectrum**: The printed spectra are submitted with the report.
- **A hand-drawn sketch of the spectrum**: Real, printed data are required.

*Source: Manual p.16.*

metadata.title: How many spin orientations does a proton (¹H) have in a magnetic fi...

variants.stem: How many spin orientations does a proton (¹H) have in a magnetic field?
variants.explanation:
**Two.** The proton has spin 1/2: aligned with or against the applied field, with a small energy gap.

Why the others fail:
- **Three**: Three orientations belong to deuterium (spin 1).
- **One**: With a single state there would be no transitions to observe.
- **Zero**: A nucleus with no orientations, like ¹²C, cannot be studied.

*Source: Manual p.16 and footnote 1; p.23.*

options.label: Two
Three
One
Zero

variants.stem: How many spin orientations does deuterium (²H) have?
variants.explanation:
**Three.** Deuterium has spin 1, giving 2I + 1 = 3 orientations.

Why the others fail:
- **Two**: That is the proton.
- **One**: No nucleus with spin has just one orientation.
- **Four**: Not for a spin-1 nucleus.

*Source: Manual p.16 and footnote 1; p.23.*

options.label: Three
Two
One
Four

variants.stem: Why can carbon-12 not be studied by NMR?
variants.explanation:
**Its nucleus has no spin, so there are no orientations in a field.** Only nuclei with spin give an NMR signal; ¹³C, ¹⁹F and ³¹P do.

Why the others fail:
- **It has too many electrons**: The number of electrons is irrelevant; the nucleus must have spin.
- **It is too heavy to be affected by a magnetic field**: Mass is not the issue.
- **It always forms bonds that cancel its signal**: Nothing cancels; there is simply no signal to cancel.

*Source: Manual p.16 and footnote 1; p.23.*

options.label: Its nucleus has no spin, so there are no orientations in a field
It has too many electrons
It is too heavy to be affected by a magnetic field
It always forms bonds that cancel its signal

variants.stem: Which nuclei can be studied by NMR, according to the manual?
variants.explanation:
**Any nucleus with spin, for example ¹³C, ¹⁹F and ³¹P (as well as ¹H).** The manual lists these three as other nuclei.

Why the others fail:
- **Only ¹H**: Other nuclei with spin work too.
- **Only elements with an odd number of protons**: The rule is nuclear spin, not proton parity as such.
- **¹²C and ¹⁶O**: These have no nuclear spin.

*Source: Manual p.16 and footnote 1; p.23.*

metadata.title: The CBC NMR spectrometers run at 300, 400 and 500 MHz. Which machin...

variants.stem: The CBC NMR spectrometers run at 300, 400 and 500 MHz. Which machine has the most powerful magnet?
variants.explanation:
**The 500 MHz machine.** The higher the frequency, the stronger the magnet.

Why the others fail:
- **The 300 MHz machine**: It has the weakest magnet of the three.
- **They are all the same; frequency is set by the software**: The frequency is set by the magnet strength.
- **The 400 MHz machine, because it is the most common**: Numbers of machines do not rank their field.

*Source: Manual pp.16-17 and footnote 4.*

options.label: The 500 MHz machine
The 300 MHz machine
They are all the same; frequency is set by the software
The 400 MHz machine, because it is the most common

metadata.title: Why is NMR chemical shift quoted in ppm (δ) and not in Hz?

variants.stem: Why is NMR chemical shift quoted in ppm (δ) and not in Hz?
variants.explanation:
**δ is the same on every spectrometer, whereas a shift in Hz would depend on the magnet.** The protons of acetone come at δ 2.1 on every machine.

Why the others fail:
- **Hz cannot be measured on an NMR spectrometer**: Frequencies are measured; they are simply machine-dependent.
- **ppm is a more accurate unit**: Accuracy is not the reason; independence from the machine is.
- **To make the TMS peak positive**: TMS is defined as zero.

*Source: Manual p.17 and footnote 4.*

options.label: δ is the same on every spectrometer, whereas a shift in Hz would depend on the magnet
Hz cannot be measured on an NMR spectrometer
ppm is a more accurate unit
To make the TMS peak positive

metadata.title: Which compound defines δ = 0 in ¹H NMR?

variants.perspectiveLabel: The δ scale, TMS and τ
variants.stem: Which compound defines δ = 0 in ¹H NMR?
variants.explanation:
**Tetramethylsilane, Me₄Si.** Zero is arbitrarily set as the shift of the protons in TMS.

Why the others fail:
- **Silicon tetrahydride**: It is not the reference compound.
- **Trimethylsilanol**: It carries an OH and is not the standard.
- **Tetramethoxysilane**: The reference has methyl groups on silicon, not methoxy groups.

*Source: Manual p.17 and footnotes 3-4.*

variants.perspectiveLabel: The δ scale, TMS and τ
variants.stem: In which direction is chemical shift plotted along the δ axis?
variants.explanation:
**From right to left, so the highest δ is on the left (downfield).** Zero (TMS) is at the right (upfield).

Why the others fail:
- **From left to right, with zero on the left**: That is how the old τ scale ran.
- **In both directions, depending on the machine**: The convention is fixed.
- **It is not plotted; only the intensities are plotted**: Position along the axis is the chemical shift.

*Source: Manual p.17 and footnotes 3-4.*

variants.stem: The old τ scale is related to δ by:
variants.explanation:
**δ = 10 − τ.** τ runs left to right, with TMS at 10.

Why the others fail:
- **δ = τ**: The two scales run in opposite directions.
- **δ = 10 + τ**: The sign is reversed.
- **δ = 1/τ**: The relation is linear, not reciprocal.

*Source: Manual p.17 and footnotes 3-4.*

variants.stem: A proton signal appears at τ 2.7 on an old spectrum. What is its δ?
variants.explanation:
**δ 7.3.** δ = 10 − 2.7 = 7.3, the aromatic region.

Why the others fail:
- **δ 2.7**: τ and δ are different scales.
- **δ 12.7**: This adds instead of subtracting.
- **δ −7.3**: The two scales do not differ by a sign.

*Source: Manual p.17 and footnotes 3-4.*

metadata.title: A spectrum recorded in CDCl₃ has a small singlet at δ 7.26. What is...

variants.perspectiveLabel: Deuterated solvents and the residual peak
variants.stem: A spectrum recorded in CDCl₃ has a small singlet at δ 7.26. What is it?
variants.explanation:
**Residual CHCl₃ in the solvent, since CDCl₃ is not 100% deuterated.** The solvent is deuterated so its protons do not swamp the spectrum, but a trace of CHCl₃ remains.

Why the others fail:
- **A benzene ring in your product**: A small singlet at exactly the solvent position is most likely the solvent signal, not your compound.
- **Tetramethylsilane**: TMS appears at δ 0.
- **Water**: Water appears at a different shift (about 1.6 in CDCl₃).

*Source: Manual p.21 footnote 9.*

variants.perspectiveLabel: Deuterated solvents and the residual peak
variants.stem: Why are NMR spectra recorded in deuterated solvents?
variants.explanation:
**So that the solvent protons do not swamp the signals of the dilute sample.** Solutions are dilute, so ordinary solvent would give an enormous peak.

Why the others fail:
- **Because deuterium couples to every proton**: Deuterium is not seen in a ¹H spectrum.
- **To lower the boiling point of the sample**: Deuteration does not do this.
- **Because normal solvents react with the magnet**: There is no such reaction; it is a signal issue.

variants.explanation:
**d₆-DMSO.** The manual lists D₂O, d₆-DMSO, d₆-acetone, d₆-benzene and d₄-methanol as other deuterated solvents.

variants.explanation:
**Carbon tetrachloride, because it contains no hydrogen.** With no protons, it gave no ¹H signal of its own.

Why the others fail:
- **Ordinary water**: Water gives a big proton signal.
- **Ordinary hexane**: It gives its own strong signals.

metadata.title: Among CH₃I, CH₃Br, CH₃Cl, CH₃OH and CH₃F, which methyl protons come...

variants.stem: Among CH₃I, CH₃Br, CH₃Cl, CH₃OH and CH₃F, which methyl protons come at the highest chemical shift (δ 4.27)?
variants.explanation:
**CH₃F.** Fluorine is the most electronegative, pulling the most electron density away and deshielding the protons the most.

Why the others fail:
- **CH₃I**: Iodine is the least electronegative of the halogens here, so these protons are the least deshielded (δ 2.16).
- **CH₃Cl**: Chlorine deshields less than fluorine (δ 3.06).
- **CH₃OH**: Oxygen is less electronegative than fluorine (δ 3.39).

*Source: Manual p.18 (CH₃X table).*

options.label: CH₃F
CH₃I
CH₃Cl
CH₃OH

variants.stem: Why does Me₄Si have a lower δ than any CH₃X where X is more electronegative than silicon?
variants.explanation:
**Silicon is electropositive, so it donates electron density and the protons are shielded.** Electropositive atoms increase shielding, electronegative atoms decrease it.

Why the others fail:
- **Silicon is more electronegative than carbon**: Silicon (1.8) is less electronegative than carbon.
- **TMS has no protons**: It has twelve equivalent protons.
- **Silicon has a nuclear spin that cancels the signal**: The cause is shielding, not spin.

*Source: Manual p.18 (CH₃X table).*

variants.stem: Methyl acetate (an ester, OCH₃ at about δ 3.67) and methanol (δ 3.39): why is the ester methoxy at a higher shift?
variants.explanation:
**The carbonyl group makes the oxygen pull more electron density, so the methyl protons are further deshielded.** More electronegative character nearby gives a bigger downfield shift.

Why the others fail:
- **The ester has more protons**: The number of protons in the molecule does not set the shift of one environment.
- **The methanol OH shields the methyl group**: The OH does not shield; it is the extra electron withdrawal in the ester that matters.
- **The solvent changes the shift only**: The difference is a real structural effect.

*Source: Manual p.18 (CH₃X table).*

variants.stem: In 1-propanol the CH₂ next to oxygen comes at δ 3.49, the middle CH₂ at 1.53 and the CH₃ at 0.93. What does this show?
variants.explanation:
**The deshielding effect of an electronegative atom falls off with distance.** The effect behaves like the inductive effect: strongest on the nearest protons.

Why the others fail:
- **The CH₃ is closest to the oxygen**: It is the farthest, which is why it is the most shielded.
- **Electronegative atoms increase shielding at a distance**: The opposite: the effect decreases but is still deshielding.
- **All three environments are equivalent**: They give three different shifts.

*Source: Manual p.18 (CH₃X table).*

options.label: The deshielding effect of an electronegative atom falls off with distance
The CH₃ is closest to the oxygen
Electronegative atoms increase shielding at a distance
All three environments are equivalent

metadata.title: CH₃Cl, CH₂Cl₂ and CHCl₃ have shifts of 3.06, 5.33 and 7.24. What pr...

variants.stem: CH₃Cl, CH₂Cl₂ and CHCl₃ have shifts of 3.06, 5.33 and 7.24. What principle does this illustrate?
variants.explanation:
**Deshielding effects of electronegative atoms add up with each extra chlorine.** Each additional Cl on the carbon moves the proton further downfield.

Why the others fail:
- **Each chlorine shields the remaining protons**: Shielding would lower δ; the values rise.
- **Chemical shift is independent of substitution**: It clearly depends on it.
- **Coupling to chlorine moves the signal**: Chlorine does not couple to protons here; the shift change is an inductive effect.

*Source: Manual p.19 (CH₃Cl, CH₂Cl₂, CHCl₃).*

options.label: Deshielding effects of electronegative atoms add up with each extra chlorine
Each chlorine shields the remaining protons
Chemical shift is independent of substitution
Coupling to chlorine moves the signal

variants.stem: Which proton comes at the highest δ?
variants.explanation:
**The H in CHCl₃.** It has three chlorines, giving the largest cumulative deshielding (δ 7.24).

Why the others fail:
- **The H in CH₃Cl**: It has only one chlorine (δ 3.06).
- **The H in CH₂Cl₂**: It has two chlorines (δ 5.33).
- **They are the same**: The shifts differ by several ppm.

*Source: Manual p.19 (CH₃Cl, CH₂Cl₂, CHCl₃).*

options.label: The H in CHCl₃
The H in CH₃Cl
The H in CH₂Cl₂

metadata.title: Why do benzene protons resonate at δ 7.26 whereas cyclohexane proto...

variants.stem: Why do benzene protons resonate at δ 7.26 whereas cyclohexane protons are at about 1.44?
variants.explanation:
**The applied field induces a ring current in the π electrons, which reinforces the field at the protons outside the ring and deshields them.** Outside the ring the induced field is parallel to the applied field.

Why the others fail:
- **Benzene has more electronegative atoms**: It has none; the difference is the π system.
- **Cyclohexane protons are close to carbon and so shielded by the nucleus**: Both have C-H bonds; the π ring current explains the shift difference.
- **Benzene is a liquid and cyclohexane a gas**: Physical state is unrelated to the effect.

*Source: Manual pp.18-19.*

options.label: The applied field induces a ring current in the π electrons, which reinforces the field at the protons outside the ring and deshields them
Benzene has more electronegative atoms
Cyclohexane protons are close to carbon and so shielded by the nucleus
Benzene is a liquid and cyclohexane a gas

variants.stem: In [18]annulene the outer protons come at δ +9 and the inner protons at δ −3. What explains the inner protons?
variants.explanation:
**Inside the ring the induced field opposes the applied field, so the inner protons are strongly shielded.** This is the corollary of the ring current: field lines run opposite inside the ring.

Why the others fail:
- **The inner protons are attached to electronegative atoms**: All protons are on carbon; the cause is the ring current.
- **The inner protons are exchanging with solvent**: They are C-H protons and do not exchange.
- **They are deuterated**: Nothing is deuterated in the question.

*Source: Manual pp.18-19.*

options.label: Inside the ring the induced field opposes the applied field, so the inner protons are strongly shielded
The inner protons are attached to electronegative atoms
The inner protons are exchanging with solvent
They are deuterated

variants.stem: At -100 °C the axial and equatorial protons of cyclohexane come at 1.1 and 1.6 ppm, but at room temperature a single signal appears at 1.44. Why?
variants.explanation:
**The ring flips so fast at room temperature that the spectrometer sees a time-averaged signal.** Axial and equatorial protons interconvert faster than the NMR timescale, so one averaged signal appears.

Why the others fail:
- **At room temperature the axial and equatorial protons become chemically identical in structure**: They are still different positions; it is the rapid interconversion that averages them.
- **The magnet is weaker at room temperature**: Field strength is fixed; temperature changes the ring-flip rate.
- **The extra protons come from the solvent**: The solvent plays no part in the averaging.

*Source: Manual pp.18-19.*

options.label: The ring flips so fast at room temperature that the spectrometer sees a time-averaged signal
At room temperature the axial and equatorial protons become chemically identical in structure
The magnet is weaker at room temperature
The extra protons come from the solvent

variants.stem: Why is [18]annulene aromatic?
variants.explanation:
**It has 18 π electrons, which fits 4n + 2 with n = 4.** The annulene shows the ring-current shifts expected of an aromatic system.

Why the others fail:
- **It has 18 carbons, which is a multiple of 4n**: Hückel aromaticity requires 4n + 2 π electrons, not 4n.
- **It has no π electrons**: It has a conjugated system of 18 π electrons.
- **It contains a benzene ring**: It is a single large ring, not a substituted benzene.

*Source: Manual pp.18-19.*

options.label: It has 18 π electrons, which fits 4n + 2 with n = 4
It has 18 carbons, which is a multiple of 4n
It has no π electrons
It contains a benzene ring

variants.stem: Which of these protons would come at the highest chemical shift?
variants.explanation:
**A carboxylic acid O-H, about δ 12.** The acidic OH is strongly deshielded and broad.

Why the others fail:
- **An aldehyde C-H, about δ 10**: It is high but lower than the carboxylic acid.
- **An aromatic C-H, about δ 7**: It is lower than aldehydes and acids.
- **A CH₃ next to a C=O, about δ 2.1**: It is far upfield of those above.

*Source: Manual p.17 (shift scale figure); typical values.*

variants.perspectiveLabel: Approximate shifts of common proton types
variants.stem: Put these in increasing order of chemical shift: CH₃C=O, ArH, RCH₂OH, TMS.
variants.explanation:
**TMS < CH₃C=O < RCH₂OH < ArH.** About 0, 2.1, 3.5 and 7.3 ppm respectively.

Why the others fail:
- **ArH < RCH₂OH < CH₃C=O < TMS**: This is the reverse order.
- **TMS < RCH₂OH < CH₃C=O < ArH**: The acetyl methyl (2.1) is below the CH₂OH (3.5).
- **CH₃C=O < TMS < ArH < RCH₂OH**: TMS is at zero, the lowest.

*Source: Manual p.17 (shift scale figure); typical values.*

variants.stem: A singlet integrating for three protons appears at δ 3.8 in methyl crotonate. Which group is it?
variants.explanation:
**The OCH₃ of the ester.** It is the easiest signal to assign: a methyl next to oxygen with no neighbouring protons.

Why the others fail:
- **The C4 methyl on the alkene**: It appears near δ 1.9 and is split.
- **An alkene proton**: Alkene protons are near δ 6-7 and integrate for one each.
- **The residual solvent peak**: CHCl₃ would be at δ 7.26 and integrate for much less.

*Source: Manual p.17 (shift scale figure); typical values.*

metadata.title: A proton has two equivalent neighbouring protons on the adjacent ca...

variants.perspectiveLabel: The n+1 rule and Pascal ratios
variants.stem: A proton has two equivalent neighbouring protons on the adjacent carbon. What multiplicity will it show?
variants.explanation:
**A triplet (1:2:1).** N = 2 neighbours gives N + 1 = 3 lines in the ratio 1:2:1.

Why the others fail:
- **A doublet**: A doublet arises from a single neighbour.
- **A quartet**: Three neighbours are needed for a quartet.
- **A singlet**: Coupling to neighbouring protons splits the signal.

*Source: Manual pp.20-21.*

options.label: A triplet (1:2:1)
A doublet
A quartet
A singlet

variants.perspectiveLabel: The n+1 rule and Pascal ratios
variants.stem: The CH proton of isopropanol is next to six equivalent protons. What multiplicity does it show?
variants.explanation:
**A septet (seven lines).** 6 + 1 = 7.

Why the others fail:
- **A sextet**: That would need five neighbours.
- **A sextuplet of doublets**: The OH usually exchanges and does not split the CH.
- **A triplet**: A triplet needs only two neighbours.

*Source: Manual pp.20-21.*

options.label: A septet (seven lines)
A sextet
A sextuplet of doublets
A triplet

variants.perspectiveLabel: The n+1 rule and Pascal ratios
variants.stem: What is the intensity ratio of the lines of a quartet?
variants.explanation:
**1:3:3:1.** Pascal's triangle gives the line intensities for three equivalent neighbours.

Why the others fail:
- **1:2:1**: That is a triplet.
- **1:1:1:1**: That is a doublet of doublets with two different couplings, not a quartet from three equivalent neighbours.
- **1:4:6:4:1**: That is a pentet.

*Source: Manual pp.20-21.*

variants.perspectiveLabel: The n+1 rule and Pascal ratios
variants.stem: A signal has 5 lines with intensities 1:4:6:4:1. How many equivalent neighbouring protons are there?
variants.explanation:
**Four.** A pentet means N + 1 = 5, so N = 4.

Why the others fail:
- **Five**: Five neighbours would give a sextet.
- **Three**: Three neighbours give a quartet.
- **Six**: Six neighbours give a septet.

*Source: Manual pp.20-21.*

options.label: Four
Five
Three
Six

variants.perspectiveLabel: The n+1 rule and Pascal ratios
variants.stem: An ethyl group (CH₃CH₂-) is attached to something with no hydrogens on the neighbouring atom. What does its ¹H spectrum look like?
variants.explanation:
**A triplet for the CH₃ (coupled to the two protons of the CH₂) and a quartet for the CH₂ (coupled to the three protons of the CH₃), integrating 3:2.** Each group is split by the other's protons.

Why the others fail:
- **A quartet for the CH₃ and a triplet for the CH₂**: The splitting is the other way round: the CH₃ sees two protons, so it is a triplet.
- **Two singlets integrating 3:2**: The groups are neighbours and do couple.
- **A single peak integrating 5**: The CH₃ and CH₂ protons are in different environments.

*Source: Manual pp.20-21.*

metadata.title: The ¹H NMR of 1,2-dichloroethane is a singlet but 1-bromo-2-chloroe...

variants.stem: The ¹H NMR of 1,2-dichloroethane is a singlet but 1-bromo-2-chloroethane shows two triplets. Why?
variants.explanation:
**Coupling is seen only between chemically non-equivalent protons; in ClCH₂CH₂Cl all four protons are equivalent, in ClCH₂CH₂Br the two CH₂ groups differ.** In the second molecule each CH₂ is split into a triplet by the other.

Why the others fail:
- **Bromine couples to protons but chlorine does not**: Halogen coupling to H is not what is being seen here.
- **Dichloroethane has fewer protons**: Both have four protons.
- **The spectrometer cannot split a four-proton signal**: The instrument can; the protons are simply equivalent and do not split each other.

*Source: Manual p.20.*

options.label: Coupling is seen only between chemically non-equivalent protons; in ClCH₂CH₂Cl all four protons are equivalent, in ClCH₂CH₂Br the two CH₂ groups differ

metadata.source: Manual p.20 and footnote 10; counting by symmetry

variants.stem: How many different proton signals does the ¹H NMR of methyl crotonate (CH₃CH=CHCO₂CH₃) show?
variants.explanation:
**Four.** OCH₃, the C4 methyl, H2 and H3 are four distinct environments.

Why the others fail:
- **Two**: The alkene protons and both methyls are in different environments.
- **Three**: H2 and H3 are different, so there are four, not three.
- **Seven**: Equivalent protons within a methyl count once.

*Source: Manual p.20 and footnote 10; counting by symmetry.*

options.label: Four
Two
Three
Seven

variants.stem: Diisopropyl ether and 2-chloropropane both show methyl and methine signals. What does integration give for each?
variants.explanation:
**Both give a 6:1 ratio (12:2 for the ether), so integration alone cannot tell them apart.** The manual points out that both show a 6:1 pattern; their shifts and the number of protons differ.

Why the others fail:
- **3:1 for the ether and 6:1 for the chloride**: Both have two methyls on each isopropyl group, giving 6:1.
- **1:1 for both**: Methyl and methine integrate 6:1.
- **The ether shows a single peak**: It has two distinct environments.

*Source: Manual p.20 and footnote 10; counting by symmetry.*

options.label: Both give a 6:1 ratio (12:2 for the ether), so integration alone cannot tell them apart
3:1 for the ether and 6:1 for the chloride

variants.stem: Which molecule shows a single ¹H NMR signal?
variants.explanation:
**Neopentane, C(CH₃)₄.** All twelve protons are equivalent, so there is a single singlet.

Why the others fail:
- **1-Bromo-2-chloroethane**: Two different CH₂ groups give two triplets.
- **Methyl crotonate**: Four different environments.
- **Isopropanol**: The methyls, the CH and the OH are different.

*Source: Manual p.20 and footnote 10; counting by symmetry.*

metadata.source: Manual p.21 (J ranges) and p.19 footnote 6 (long-range coupling)

variants.stem: Two alkene protons on a 1,2-disubstituted double bond are cis. What range of coupling constant is typical, according to the manual?
variants.explanation:
**About 10-12 Hz.** The manual gives about 10-12 Hz for cis and often 15-18 Hz for trans.

Why the others fail:
- **About 15-18 Hz**: That is the trans range.
- **About 0-1 Hz**: That is the size of a weak long-range coupling, not a cis vicinal coupling.
- **About 40 Hz**: H-H couplings do not reach that size.

*Source: Manual p.21 (J ranges) and p.19 footnote 6 (long-range coupling).*

About 15-18 Hz
About 0-1 Hz

variants.stem: A 1,2-disubstituted alkene shows J = 16 Hz between its two alkene protons. What geometry does it have?
variants.explanation:
**Trans (E).** Trans couplings are larger, 15-18 Hz; cis is about 10-12 Hz.

Why the others fail:
- **Cis (Z)**: Cis couplings are smaller (about 10-12 Hz).
- **Geminal**: The two protons are on different carbons.
- **It cannot be told from J**: J is the standard way to tell them apart.

*Source: Manual p.21 (J ranges) and p.19 footnote 6 (long-range coupling).*

options.label: Trans (E)

variants.stem: Over how many bonds does coupling usually occur between protons?
variants.explanation:
**Two or three bonds (²J or ³J).** Coupling through more bonds (long range) is less common.

Why the others fail:
- **Only through one bond**: Protons are not directly bonded to each other.
- **Always through six or more bonds**: Coupling falls off quickly with distance.
- **Through space only, never through bonds**: The coupling in the manual is transmitted through bonds.

*Source: Manual p.21 (J ranges) and p.19 footnote 6 (long-range coupling).*

Only through one bond
Always through six or more bonds
Through space only, never through bonds

variants.stem: Which of these is an example of long-range coupling given in the manual?
variants.explanation:
**Allylic coupling in alkenes and meta coupling in aromatics (both ⁴J).** Both are four-bond couplings; alkynes can show ⁴J or ⁵J.

Why the others fail:
- **Geminal coupling in CH₂**: That is ²J, a two-bond coupling.
- **Vicinal coupling in an ethyl group**: That is ³J, the normal case.
- **Coupling between ¹²C and ¹H**: ¹²C has no spin.

*Source: Manual p.21 (J ranges) and p.19 footnote 6 (long-range coupling).*

variants.stem: What is the possible range of ¹H-¹H coupling constants stated in the manual?
variants.explanation:
**0 to 18 Hz.** Couplings are never much larger than this.

Why the others fail:
- **0 to 1 Hz**: Many couplings are much larger.
- **50 to 500 Hz**: These are far outside the range.
- **They are the same for all protons**: J depends on the geometry and the bonds between the protons.

*Source: Manual p.21 (J ranges) and p.19 footnote 6 (long-range coupling).*

metadata.title: In methyl crotonate (CH₃-CH=CH-CO₂CH₃), H3 is next to both H2 and t...

variants.stem: In methyl crotonate (CH₃-CH=CH-CO₂CH₃), H3 is next to both H2 and the C4 methyl. What does its signal look like?
variants.explanation:
**A doublet of quartets (dq): a doublet from H2 and a quartet from the three methyl protons.** The two couplings differ, so the splittings are analysed step by step.

Why the others fail:
- **A triplet**: H3 has two different kinds of neighbour, so a simple triplet is not expected.
- **A doublet of doublets (dd)**: That would mean only two single-proton neighbours; the three methyl protons give a quartet, not a doublet.
- **A singlet**: H3 has neighbours and must be split.

*Source: Manual pp.21-22 (methyl crotonate).*

options.label: A doublet of quartets (dq): a doublet from H2 and a quartet from the three methyl protons
A triplet
A doublet of doublets (dd)
A singlet

variants.stem: H2 of methyl crotonate is also a doublet of quartets. What causes the small quartet?
variants.explanation:
**Long-range (allylic) coupling to the three protons of the C4 methyl.** The allylic coupling is small, so the quartet lines are close together.

Why the others fail:
- **Coupling to the OCH₃ protons**: They are too many bonds away and separated by the ester.
- **Coupling to the solvent**: Solvent coupling is not seen in this way.
- **Coupling to the ¹³C nucleus**: ¹³C is only 1% abundant and gives tiny satellites, not a quartet.

*Source: Manual pp.21-22 (methyl crotonate).*

variants.stem: The C4 methyl group of methyl crotonate appears as a doublet of doublets (dd). Which couplings are involved?
variants.explanation:
**A larger coupling to H3 (three bonds) and a smaller allylic coupling to H2 (four bonds).** The two different one-proton neighbours give two different splittings.

Why the others fail:
- **Coupling to both OCH₃ protons**: The OCH₃ is a distant singlet.
- **Coupling to the three protons on itself**: Equivalent protons do not couple to each other.
- **Coupling to the carbonyl carbon**: No proton-carbon coupling is observed here.

*Source: Manual pp.21-22 (methyl crotonate).*

options.label: A larger coupling to H3 (three bonds) and a smaller allylic coupling to H2 (four bonds)

variants.stem: In what ratio do the integrals of H3, H2, the C4 methyl and the OCH₃ of methyl crotonate fall (from low field to high field: H3, H2, OCH₃, C4-CH₃)?
variants.explanation:
**1 : 1 : 3 : 3.** Integrals count protons: one each for the alkene protons and three each for the two methyls (the manual's integrated spectrum reads about 1.0 : 1.0 : 3.2 : 3.0).

Why the others fail:
- **1 : 1 : 2 : 2**: A methyl group has three protons, not two.
- **3 : 3 : 1 : 1**: This reverses the order; the alkene protons are the single-proton signals.
- **1 : 1 : 1 : 1**: Methyl signals are three times larger than single-proton signals.

*Source: Manual pp.21-22 (methyl crotonate).*

metadata.title: What does the integral of a ¹H NMR signal tell you?

variants.stem: What does the integral of a ¹H NMR signal tell you?
variants.explanation:
**The relative number of protons giving that signal (a ratio, not an absolute count).** Each proton emits in the same way, so signal size is proportional to the number of protons.

Why the others fail:
- **The number of neighbouring protons**: That comes from the splitting pattern.
- **The absolute number of protons in the molecule**: Integrals form ratios; you scale them with a known group.
- **The coupling constant**: J comes from the line spacing.

*Source: Manual p.22 and footnote 10.*

options.label: The relative number of protons giving that signal (a ratio, not an absolute count)
The number of neighbouring protons
The absolute number of protons in the molecule
The coupling constant

metadata.title: A mixture of compound A and compound B shows an A singlet (3H per m...

variants.stem: A mixture of compound A and compound B shows an A singlet (3H per molecule) of integral 6.0 and a B singlet (1H per molecule) of integral 2.0. What is the A:B mole ratio?
variants.explanation:
**1:1.** Normalise per proton: A gives 6.0/3 = 2.0 and B gives 2.0/1 = 2.0, so they are present in equal amounts.

Why the others fail:
- **3:1**: This compares raw integrals without dividing by the number of protons each represents.
- **1:3**: This divides in the wrong direction.
- **6:1**: The integrals have not been normalised per proton.

*Source: Manual p.22 footnote 10.*

metadata.title: Why do OH and NH protons often appear as broad singlets with no vis...
metadata.source: Manual p.22 (exchange); p.17 (shift chart, acid OH near 12)

variants.stem: Why do OH and NH protons often appear as broad singlets with no visible coupling?
variants.explanation:
**They exchange rapidly between molecules, often faster than the NMR timescale.** Rapid exchange averages out the coupling and broadens the signal.

Why the others fail:
- **They have no neighbouring protons**: Many do; exchange is the reason they are not seen coupling.
- **Oxygen and nitrogen have spin 1/2 and decouple them**: The explanation is proton exchange.
- **They resonate at exactly the same position as TMS**: They appear at variable positions, often downfield.

*Source: Manual p.22 (exchange); p.17 (shift chart, acid OH near 12).*

variants.stem: The same OH proton is seen at different chemical shifts in different samples of the same compound. Why?
variants.explanation:
**It exchanges with other OH groups and traces of water, so its position depends on concentration, solvent and water content.** This variability is a hallmark of exchangeable protons.

Why the others fail:
- **The spectrometer has drifted between samples**: Drift is small and would affect all signals equally.
- **The compound has changed structure between samples**: The structure is the same; the environment of the OH varies.
- **OH protons have random shifts that carry no information**: They are informative, just variable.

*Source: Manual p.22 (exchange); p.17 (shift chart, acid OH near 12).*

variants.stem: Which signal in a ¹H spectrum is most likely to be a broad singlet near δ 12?
variants.explanation:
**A carboxylic acid O-H.** Acid protons are strongly deshielded and exchange.

Why the others fail:
- **An aromatic C-H**: It is sharp and near 7-8.
- **A methyl on a ring**: It is sharp and near 2.3.
- **An aldehyde C-H**: It gives a sharper signal near 10 (and may be a doublet or singlet).

*Source: Manual p.22 (exchange); p.17 (shift chart, acid OH near 12).*

metadata.title: A doublet has two lines 7.0 Hz apart. On a 300 MHz spectrometer, ho...

variants.stem: A doublet has two lines 7.0 Hz apart. On a 300 MHz spectrometer, how far apart are they in δ?
variants.explanation:
**0.023 ppm (7.0 / 300).** Divide the separation in Hz by the spectrometer frequency in MHz to get ppm.

Why the others fail:
- **7.0 ppm**: This confuses Hz with ppm.
- **2100 ppm**: This multiplies by 300 instead of dividing.
- **0.0014 ppm**: This divides by 5000, not by 300.

*Source: Manual pp.16-17, footnote 4; Hz/ppm arithmetic.*

options.label: 7.0 ppm
2100 ppm

variants.stem: The same compound is run at 300 MHz and at 500 MHz. What changes?
variants.explanation:
**Shifts in ppm and J in Hz stay the same, but the signals are spread over more Hz, so the multiplets overlap less.** δ is independent of the machine; a stronger field spreads the same δ range over more Hz.

Why the others fail:
- **The shifts in ppm change, but J does not**: Both δ and J are field-independent.
- **J in Hz increases in proportion to the frequency**: J is a property of the molecule.
- **Nothing at all, including the resolution**: Higher field gives better dispersion.

*Source: Manual pp.16-17, footnote 4; Hz/ppm arithmetic.*

options.label: Shifts in ppm and J in Hz stay the same, but the signals are spread over more Hz, so the multiplets overlap less
The shifts in ppm change, but J does not

variants.stem: Using the databook, which of these carbonyl types has the LOWEST wavenumber range?
variants.explanation:
**An α,β-unsaturated ketone (1685-1660 cm⁻¹).** Conjugation lowers the C=O stretch; the saturated ketone is 1725-1705 and the aryl ketone 1700-1680.

Why the others fail:

- **A five-membered ring ketone (1750-1740 cm⁻¹)**: Ring strain raises the frequency.

metadata.title: In Expt 1A, 4-aminophenol reacts with acetic anhydride. Which react...

variants.stem: In Expt 1A, 4-aminophenol reacts with acetic anhydride. Which reaction class and site of reaction is correct?
variants.explanation:
**Nucleophilic acyl substitution on nitrogen (N-acetylation); the amine is a better nucleophile than the phenol OH.** The NH₂ attacks a carbonyl of the anhydride, expelling acetate, to give the amide paracetamol and acetic acid. *(Beyond the manual: standard organic or analytical chemistry.)*

Why the others fail:
- **Electrophilic aromatic substitution on the ring**: The anhydride acylates the heteroatom nucleophile; the ring is not attacked under these conditions.
- **Esterification of the phenol OH**: The OH is the weaker nucleophile; the amide forms instead.
- **Aldol condensation**: There is no enolisable carbonyl component acting as a nucleophile here.

*Source: Manual p.29.*

variants.stem: What is the by-product of 4-aminophenol + acetic anhydride, and what happens to it?
variants.explanation:
**Acetic acid; it stays dissolved in the aqueous mother liquor and is washed away.** One acetyl group goes to the amine and the other leaves as acetic acid. *(Beyond the manual: standard organic or analytical chemistry.)*

Why the others fail:
- **Sodium acetate; it crystallises with the product**: No sodium is present at this stage; NaOH only appears in the later purification.
- **Hydrogen gas; it bubbles out**: No reduction occurs.
- **Water; it makes the reaction boil**: The acylation of an amine by an anhydride releases acetic acid, not water.

*Source: Manual p.29.*

variants.stem: To purify crude paracetamol you dissolve it in 2 M NaOH, filter, and then acidify the filtrate with 6 M HCl. What does this achieve?
variants.explanation:
**The phenol is deprotonated to the soluble phenoxide, so insoluble non-acidic impurities are filtered off; acid then re-forms the insoluble paracetamol.** This acid-base purification separates the product from material that is not soluble in base. *(Beyond the manual: standard organic or analytical chemistry.)*

Why the others fail:
- **The NaOH hydrolyses paracetamol to 4-aminophenol, which is then re-acetylated**: No second acetylation takes place; the base only deprotonates the phenol.
- **The HCl converts paracetamol to its hydrochloride salt, which dissolves**: The point of acidifying is to precipitate paracetamol, which comes out as a solid.
- **The NaOH removes the water of crystallisation**: It performs an acid-base separation; no hydrate is involved.

*Source: Manual p.29.*

- **The temperature drops to 0 °C**: Neutralisation of NaOH by HCl is exothermic; temperature is not the indicator.

metadata.title: What reaction type forms dibenzalacetone from benzaldehyde and acet...

variants.stem: What reaction type forms dibenzalacetone from benzaldehyde and acetone with NaOH?
variants.explanation:
**A base-catalysed crossed aldol condensation (twice), with loss of water.** The acetone enolate attacks benzaldehyde; dehydration gives a conjugated enone, and the process repeats on the other side of the acetone. *(Beyond the manual: standard organic or analytical chemistry.)*

Why the others fail:
- **A Grignard addition**: No organometallic reagent is present.
- **A Friedel-Crafts acylation**: No acylium ion or Lewis acid is involved.
- **A Cannizzaro reaction giving benzyl alcohol and benzoate**: That is a side reaction of benzaldehyde with strong base, not the aim.

*Source: Manual p.31.*

options.label: A base-catalysed crossed aldol condensation (twice), with loss of water
A Grignard addition
A Friedel-Crafts acylation
A Cannizzaro reaction giving benzyl alcohol and benzoate

metadata.title: Why does benzaldehyde act only as the electrophile in this aldol re...

variants.stem: Why does benzaldehyde act only as the electrophile in this aldol reaction?
variants.explanation:
**It has no α-hydrogens, so it cannot form an enolate and cannot condense with itself.** Acetone is the only partner that can enolise, so the crossed reaction is clean. *(Beyond the manual: standard organic or analytical chemistry.)*

Why the others fail:
- **It is too hindered to react with itself**: The key is the lack of α-hydrogens, not steric bulk.
- **It is deactivated by the ring and unreactive to nucleophiles**: Aromatic aldehydes are good electrophiles.
- **It is insoluble in ethanol**: It dissolves in ethanol.

*Source: Manual p.31.*

options.label: It has no α-hydrogens, so it cannot form an enolate and cannot condense with itself
It is too hindered to react with itself
It is deactivated by the ring and unreactive to nucleophiles
It is insoluble in ethanol

metadata.title: Why is the benzaldehyde-acetone solution added slowly, with the tem...

variants.stem: Why is the benzaldehyde-acetone solution added slowly, with the temperature held between 20 and 25 °C?
variants.explanation:
**The reaction is exothermic, and higher temperatures favour side reactions; slow addition with a cooling bath keeps it under control.** The NaOH solution is first cooled in an ice-water bath.

Why the others fail:
- **Below 20 °C the benzaldehyde freezes**: Benzaldehyde does not freeze at these temperatures.
- **Above 25 °C the ethanol boils**: Ethanol boils at about 78 °C.
- **The product only forms below 20 °C**: The target range is 20-25 °C.

*Source: Manual p.31.*

options.label: The reaction is exothermic, and higher temperatures favour side reactions; slow addition with a cooling bath keeps it under control
Below 20 °C the benzaldehyde freezes
Above 25 °C the ethanol boils
The product only forms below 20 °C

metadata.title: The procedure uses about 16.7 mmol of benzaldehyde and 8.6 mmol of ...

variants.stem: The procedure uses about 16.7 mmol of benzaldehyde and 8.6 mmol of acetone. Why is the ratio about 2:1?
variants.explanation:
**Each acetone molecule condenses with two benzaldehyde molecules, one at each α-carbon, giving the bis-benzylidene product.** Acetone is therefore the limiting reagent for the theoretical yield. *(Beyond the manual: standard organic or analytical chemistry.)*

Why the others fail:
- **One benzaldehyde per acetone is enough, so the extra is to speed the reaction**: The product contains two benzylidene units, so two benzaldehydes are needed.
- **Benzaldehyde acts as the base**: The base is NaOH.
- **Acetone is also the solvent**: Acetone is the reagent used in limited amount; ethanol/water is the solvent.

*Source: Manual p.31 (quantities).*

options.label: Each acetone molecule condenses with two benzaldehyde molecules, one at each α-carbon, giving the bis-benzylidene product
One benzaldehyde per acetone is enough, so the extra is to speed the reaction
Benzaldehyde acts as the base
Acetone is also the solvent

metadata.title: Which IR band is characteristic of dibenzalacetone, and where does ...

variants.stem: Which IR band is characteristic of dibenzalacetone, and where does it fall relative to an ordinary ketone?
variants.explanation:
**A conjugated C=O at about 1650-1685 cm⁻¹ (databook: 1685-1660 for α,β-unsaturated ketones), lower than the 1725-1705 cm⁻¹ of acetone.** Conjugation with two C=C bonds lowers the carbonyl frequency; a C=C stretch appears near 1600-1625 cm⁻¹ too. *(Beyond the manual: standard organic or analytical chemistry.)*

Why the others fail:
- **An aldehyde C-H near 2720 cm⁻¹ from unreacted benzaldehyde**: In the pure product that band should be absent, so its presence would indicate contamination.
- **A broad O-H near 3300 cm⁻¹**: There is no OH in the pure product.
- **A C=O at 1740 cm⁻¹**: That is typical of an ester.

*Source: Manual p.31; IR correlation tables.*

options.label: A conjugated C=O at about 1650-1685 cm⁻¹ (databook: 1685-1660 for α,β-unsaturated ketones), lower than the 1725-1705 cm⁻¹ of acetone
An aldehyde C-H near 2720 cm⁻¹ from unreacted benzaldehyde
A broad O-H near 3300 cm⁻¹
A C=O at 1740 cm⁻¹

metadata.title: How is crude dibenzalacetone purified, and what does the manual ask...

variants.stem: How is crude dibenzalacetone purified, and what does the manual ask you to record?
variants.explanation:
**Recrystallise from ethanol, dry in a desiccator, then measure the mp and yield, record the IR and run TLC.** The solid is collected by filtration first.

Why the others fail:
- **Distil it under reduced pressure**: It is a solid, not a distillable liquid under these conditions.
- **Run a flash column on the crude solid**: Column chromatography is Expt 7.
- **Sublime it under vacuum**: Sublimation is used in Expt 5E.

*Source: Manual p.31.*

metadata.title: What is the balanced overall change in Expt 1D?

variants.stem: What is the balanced overall change in Expt 1D?
variants.explanation:
**Zn(NO₃)₂ + 2 NaNCO + 2 py → Zn(py)₂(NCO)₂ + 2 NaNO₃.** Cyanate and pyridine both coordinate to zinc; the sodium nitrate stays in solution. *(Beyond the manual: standard organic or analytical chemistry.)*

Why the others fail:
- **Zn(NO₃)₂ + NaNCO + py → Zn(py)(NCO)₂ + NaNO₃**: This does not balance: two cyanates and two pyridines are needed per zinc.
- **Zn + 2 NaNCO + 2 py → Zn(py)₂(NCO)₂ + 2 Na**: Zinc starts as Zn(II) nitrate, not the metal, and sodium is not released as a metal.
- **Zn(NO₃)₂ + 2 py → Zn(py)₂(NO₃)₂**: This is a different complex; the cyanate is the second ligand type.

*Source: Manual p.32.*

Zn(NO₃)₂ + NaNCO + py → Zn(py)(NCO)₂ + NaNO₃
Zn + 2 NaNCO + 2 py → Zn(py)₂(NCO)₂ + 2 Na
Zn(NO₃)₂ + 2 py → Zn(py)₂(NO₃)₂

metadata.title: 3 mL of 2 M Zn(NO₃)₂ is treated with 12 mL of 1 M NaNCO. What is th...

variants.stem: 3 mL of 2 M Zn(NO₃)₂ is treated with 12 mL of 1 M NaNCO. What is the cyanate-to-zinc mole ratio?
variants.explanation:
**2:1 (12 mmol NCO⁻ to 6 mmol Zn²⁺).** This matches the formula Zn(py)₂(NCO)₂ with two cyanate ligands per zinc. *(Beyond the manual: standard organic or analytical chemistry.)*

Why the others fail:
- **1:1**: That would use 6 mL of the cyanate solution.
- **4:1**: That ratio does not follow from 12 mmol and 6 mmol.
- **1:2**: The ratio is inverted.

*Source: Manual p.32 (volumes and concentrations).*

options.label: 2:1 (12 mmol NCO⁻ to 6 mmol Zn²⁺)

metadata.title: The filtered complex is washed with ice-cold water. What does this ...

variants.stem: The filtered complex is washed with ice-cold water. What does this remove, and why cold?
variants.explanation:
**Dissolved salts such as sodium nitrate; cold water minimises loss of the slightly soluble product.** A cold wash rinses the by-product off the solid without redissolving the complex. *(Beyond the manual: standard organic or analytical chemistry.)*

Why the others fail:
- **Unreacted pyridine, which is insoluble in water**: Pyridine is miscible with water; the main contaminant is the sodium salt.
- **Unreacted zinc metal**: No zinc metal is present.
- **The wash is for cooling the product only**: It removes soluble impurities too.

*Source: Manual p.32.*

options.label: Dissolved salts such as sodium nitrate; cold water minimises loss of the slightly soluble product
Unreacted pyridine, which is insoluble in water
Unreacted zinc metal
The wash is for cooling the product only

metadata.title: What hazard does the manual give for Expt 1D?

variants.stem: What hazard does the manual give for Expt 1D?
variants.explanation:
**Pyridine is toxic: avoid inhalation and skin contact.** Dispense it in the fume cupboard with a syringe, wearing gloves.

Why the others fail:
- **Zinc nitrate is explosive when warmed to 50 °C**: The listed hazard is pyridine.
- **Sodium cyanate releases hydrogen cyanide on warming**: The manual does not say this; it warns about pyridine.
- **The reaction must be done under nitrogen**: It is carried out in water in air.

*Source: Manual p.32.*

options.label: Pyridine is toxic: avoid inhalation and skin contact
Zinc nitrate is explosive when warmed to 50 °C
Sodium cyanate releases hydrogen cyanide on warming

metadata.title: In Py₂Zn(NCO)₂ the cyanate ligands bind to zinc through which atom,...

variants.stem: In Py₂Zn(NCO)₂ the cyanate ligands bind to zinc through which atom, and what is the likely geometry at zinc?
variants.explanation:
**Through nitrogen (an isocyanate), with a tetrahedral arrangement of two pyridine N and two NCO N donors.** The drawn structure shows four nitrogen donors around zinc(II), a d¹⁰ centre that favours tetrahedral geometry. *(Beyond the manual: standard organic or analytical chemistry.)*

Why the others fail:
- **Through oxygen, with square-planar geometry**: The manual's drawing shows Zn-NCO bonds, and zinc(II) d¹⁰ is not square-planar.
- **Through carbon, with octahedral geometry**: Coordination via carbon would be a cyanide-type ligand; this is a four-coordinate complex.
- **The cyanate bridges two zinc ions in a polymer**: The manual's formula is a discrete four-coordinate complex.

*Source: Manual p.32 (structure drawn).*

options.label: Through nitrogen (an isocyanate), with a tetrahedral arrangement of two pyridine N and two NCO N donors
Through oxygen, with square-planar geometry
Through carbon, with octahedral geometry
The cyanate bridges two zinc ions in a polymer

metadata.title: Which IR band would you look for to confirm the isocyanate ligand i...

variants.stem: Which IR band would you look for to confirm the isocyanate ligand in Py₂Zn(NCO)₂?
variants.explanation:
**A strong N=C=O asymmetric stretch in the 2200-2250 cm⁻¹ region.** This cumulated-double-bond stretch is distinctive and appears in the triple-bond window. *(Beyond the manual: standard organic or analytical chemistry.)*

Why the others fail:
- **A broad O-H band near 3300 cm⁻¹**: The complex has no OH.
- **A strong C=O stretch near 1715 cm⁻¹**: There is no ketone-type carbonyl.
- **A nitro stretch near 1530 cm⁻¹**: The nitrate remained in solution as sodium nitrate.

*Source: Manual p.32; IR correlation tables.*

options.label: A strong N=C=O asymmetric stretch in the 2200-2250 cm⁻¹ region
A broad O-H band near 3300 cm⁻¹
A strong C=O stretch near 1715 cm⁻¹

metadata.title: What is 2,5-dimethoxytetrahydrofuran doing in Expt 1E?

variants.stem: What is 2,5-dimethoxytetrahydrofuran doing in Expt 1E?
variants.explanation:
**It is a masked succinaldehyde (a 1,4-dicarbonyl equivalent) that, in hot acetic acid, condenses with the sulfonamide nitrogen to build the pyrrole ring.** The acetals lose methanol under acid, and the nitrogen closes the five-membered ring, which then loses water (Clauson-Kaas pyrrole synthesis). *(Beyond the manual: standard organic or analytical chemistry.)*

Why the others fail:
- **It is the nucleophile that adds to the aromatic ring of tosylamide**: It supplies the four carbons of the pyrrole ring, not a ring substituent.
- **It is a base that deprotonates the sulfonamide**: The medium is acidic (acetic acid), not basic.
- **It is an oxidant converting the NH₂ to NO₂**: No oxidation takes place.

*Source: Manual p.33.*

options.label: It is a masked succinaldehyde (a 1,4-dicarbonyl equivalent) that, in hot acetic acid, condenses with the sulfonamide nitrogen to build the pyrrole ring
It is the nucleophile that adds to the aromatic ring of tosylamide
It is a base that deprotonates the sulfonamide
It is an oxidant converting the NH₂ to NO₂

metadata.title: About 7.6 mmol of 2,5-dimethoxytetrahydrofuran react with about 5.8...

variants.stem: About 7.6 mmol of 2,5-dimethoxytetrahydrofuran react with about 5.8 mmol of p-toluenesulfonamide. Which is the limiting reagent?
variants.explanation:
**p-Toluenesulfonamide.** It supplies the nitrogen that goes into the pyrrole and has the smaller number of moles. *(Beyond the manual: standard organic or analytical chemistry.)*

Why the others fail:
- **2,5-Dimethoxytetrahydrofuran**: There is more of it (7.6 mmol) than sulfonamide (5.8 mmol).
- **Acetic acid**: It is the solvent, in large excess.
- **They are exactly equal**: The moles differ.

*Source: Manual p.33 (quantities).*

options.label: p-Toluenesulfonamide
2,5-Dimethoxytetrahydrofuran
Acetic acid
They are exactly equal

metadata.title: After two hours at reflux the mixture is poured into 60 mL of water...

variants.stem: After two hours at reflux the mixture is poured into 60 mL of water and the solid is washed with water. What are the washings for?
variants.explanation:
**To remove acetic acid until the solid no longer smells of it, leaving the insoluble product.** The acid and water-soluble by-products stay in the aqueous phase.

Why the others fail:
- **To neutralise the product with a base**: Only water is used; there is no base.
- **To hydrolyse the sulfonamide to the pyrrole**: The pyrrole ring has already been formed; water just washes.
- **To dissolve the product for recrystallisation**: The product is insoluble in water, which is why it precipitates.

*Source: Manual p.33.*

options.label: To remove acetic acid until the solid no longer smells of it, leaving the insoluble product
To neutralise the product with a base
To hydrolyse the sulfonamide to the pyrrole
To dissolve the product for recrystallisation

metadata.title: Which set-up is right for the two-hour reflux of Expt 1E?

variants.stem: Which set-up is right for the two-hour reflux of Expt 1E?
variants.explanation:
**A round-bottom flask with a stir bar, fitted with a water-cooled reflux condenser and heated in an oil bath, with water in at the bottom.** No special ice-water is needed because acetic acid is not very volatile.

Why the others fail:
- **An open flask on a hotplate**: The solvent would evaporate and fumes escape; a reflux condenser is needed.
- **A condenser with ice-water in at the top**: Water goes in at the bottom, and ice-water is only for very volatile solvents like ether.
- **A sealed tube**: A closed system under heat could build up pressure.

*Source: Manual pp.24-25, 33.*

options.label: A round-bottom flask with a stir bar, fitted with a water-cooled reflux condenser and heated in an oil bath, with water in at the bottom
An open flask on a hotplate
A condenser with ice-water in at the top
A sealed tube

metadata.title: Which IR evidence shows the sulfonamide has become 1-tosylpyrrole?

variants.stem: Which IR evidence shows the sulfonamide has become 1-tosylpyrrole?
variants.explanation:
**The N-H stretches of the primary sulfonamide (two bands between about 3250 and 3400 cm⁻¹) disappear, and strong S=O bands remain near 1370 and 1170 cm⁻¹.** The N is now fully substituted, so there is no N-H. *(Beyond the manual: standard organic or analytical chemistry.)*

Why the others fail:
- **A new C=O band near 1700 cm⁻¹**: There is no carbonyl in the product.
- **The S=O bands disappear**: The sulfonyl group is retained.
- **A broad O-H band near 3300 cm⁻¹**: The product has no OH (a broad band would signal wet or acid-contaminated sample).

*Source: Manual p.33; IR correlation tables.*

The S=O bands disappear
A broad O-H band near 3300 cm⁻¹

metadata.title: Why is glacial acetic acid the solvent for Expt 1E?

variants.stem: Why is glacial acetic acid the solvent for Expt 1E?
variants.explanation:
**It dissolves the reagents and also supplies the acid catalyst needed to unmask the aldehyde from the acetal.** The acetal ring-opens under acid. *(Beyond the manual: standard organic or analytical chemistry.)*

Why the others fail:
- **It acts as the reducing agent**: No reduction is involved.
- **It is the source of the pyrrole nitrogen**: The nitrogen comes from the sulfonamide.
- **It protects the product from water**: Water is a by-product of the ring closure.

*Source: Manual p.33.*

metadata.title: What bonds form when benzil reacts with 1,3-diphenylacetone and KOH...

variants.stem: What bonds form when benzil reacts with 1,3-diphenylacetone and KOH in ethanol?
variants.explanation:
**Two C-C bonds in a double aldol (Knoevenagel-type) condensation, closing a five-membered ring after loss of two molecules of water.** The two CH₂ carbons of diphenylacetone attack the two carbonyls of benzil, then dehydrations give the conjugated ring. *(Beyond the manual: standard organic or analytical chemistry.)*

Why the others fail:
- **Two C-O bonds in an esterification**: No ester forms; the new bonds are C-C.
- **One C-N bond to give an imine**: No nitrogen reagent is present.
- **A Diels-Alder cycloaddition forming two C-C bonds in one step**: The product forms by base-mediated condensations, not by a concerted cycloaddition.

*Source: Manual p.34.*

metadata.title: KOH (about 2.6 mmol) is used with benzil and diphenylacetone (about...

variants.stem: KOH (about 2.6 mmol) is used with benzil and diphenylacetone (about 4.8 mmol each). What does this tell you about its role?
variants.explanation:
**It is a catalyst (substoichiometric): it generates enolates, and hydroxide is regenerated after each dehydration.** Less than one equivalent of base is enough for aldol condensations. *(Beyond the manual: standard organic or analytical chemistry.)*

Why the others fail:
- **It is the limiting reagent that sets the yield**: The yield is set by the two ketones.
- **It is consumed completely to form potassium salts**: The base is regenerated in the condensation steps.
- **It acts as the solvent**: Ethanol is the solvent.

*Source: Manual p.34 (quantities).*

metadata.title: Why is the KOH solution added with a Pasteur pipette through the to...

variants.stem: Why is the KOH solution added with a Pasteur pipette through the top of the condenser to the almost-boiling mixture, in two portions?
variants.explanation:
**The mixture froths when the base goes in, so adding the KOH in two portions through the condenser keeps it controlled without opening the hot apparatus.** The manual gives the procedure (base added in two portions through the condenser, then wait for the frothing to subside before refluxing for 15 minutes); the reason is inferred from that frothing.

Why the others fail:
- **To keep air out of the flask**: The apparatus is not under inert gas.
- **KOH only dissolves when added slowly to cold ethanol**: It is dissolved first in 1 mL of ethanol.
- **The condenser is the only neck available for a stirrer**: A stir bar is used and the condenser neck is used for addition.

*Source: Manual p.34.*

variants.stem: What is the specific warning for KOH in Expt 1F?
variants.explanation:
**KOH is corrosive, especially as a solution in ethanol.** Wear gloves and take care when pipetting.

Why the others fail:
- **KOH is only dangerous as a dry solid**: The manual says the ethanolic solution is especially corrosive.
- **KOH is flammable on contact with air**: It is not.
- **KOH is toxic only by inhalation**: The listed hazard is corrosive.

metadata.title: How is the product isolated in Expt 1F?

variants.stem: How is the product isolated in Expt 1F?
variants.explanation:
**Cool to room temperature, then to 0 °C in ice, and collect the precipitate by Buchner filtration, washing with a little cool ethanol.** The product is poorly soluble in cold ethanol and crystallises directly; no extraction is needed.

Why the others fail:
- **Extract into ether and evaporate**: No extraction is described.
- **Evaporate the ethanol on the rotavap and sublime the residue**: The product precipitates and is filtered; sublimation is Expt 5E.
- **Pour into water and extract with dichloromethane**: The procedure filters the precipitate formed on cooling.

*Source: Manual p.34.*

- **An aldehyde C-H near 2720 cm⁻¹**: No aldehyde is present.
- **A nitrile band near 2250 cm⁻¹**: No nitrile is present.

*Source: Manual p.34; IR correlation tables.*

metadata.title: What does the mixture of nitric and sulfuric acids do in Expt 5A?

variants.stem: What does the mixture of nitric and sulfuric acids do in Expt 5A?
variants.explanation:
**Sulfuric acid protonates nitric acid, which loses water to give the nitronium ion NO₂⁺, the electrophile that attacks the ring.** This is electrophilic aromatic substitution; sulfuric acid is also the medium. *(Beyond the manual: standard organic or analytical chemistry.)*

Why the others fail:
- **It oxidises the ester to a carboxylic acid**: The ester is not oxidised; the ring is nitrated.
- **It hydrolyses the methyl ester to benzoic acid**: The ester survives the cold nitrating mixture.
- **It acts as a nucleophile attacking the carbonyl carbon**: The nitrating agent is an electrophile and it attacks the ring.

*Source: Manual p.35.*

metadata.title: Why does the nitro group enter the meta position of methyl benzoate?

variants.stem: Why does the nitro group enter the meta position of methyl benzoate?
variants.explanation:
**The ester is an electron-withdrawing, deactivating group, and attack at the meta position avoids placing positive charge next to it in the intermediate.** Ortho and para attack give a less stable intermediate, so meta is the least disfavoured. *(Beyond the manual: standard organic or analytical chemistry.)*

Why the others fail:
- **The ester is an electron-donating group that directs ortho and para**: The carbonyl withdraws electrons, so it directs meta.
- **The nitronium ion is too large to attack ortho or para**: Sterics play a minor role; the electronic effect decides.
- **Meta is the only position that is not deactivated**: All positions are deactivated; meta is deactivated least.

*Source: Manual p.35.*

options.label: The ester is an electron-withdrawing, deactivating group, and attack at the meta position avoids placing positive charge next to it in the intermediate
The ester is an electron-donating group that directs ortho and para
The nitronium ion is too large to attack ortho or para
Meta is the only position that is not deactivated

metadata.title: Why is the temperature held between 5 and 15 °C while the nitrating...

variants.stem: Why is the temperature held between 5 and 15 °C while the nitrating mixture is added?
variants.explanation:
**Nitration is strongly exothermic, and a hot mixture risks over-nitration and runaway; the acids are added slowly with cooling.** The sulfuric acid is cooled to 0 °C at the start.

Why the others fail:
- **Nitric acid freezes below 15 °C**: It does not freeze there.
- **Higher temperatures stop the nitronium ion forming**: Higher temperature increases the rate; the aim is control and selectivity.
- **The product decomposes below 5 °C**: The product does not decompose at low temperature.

*Source: Manual p.35.*
